about: Every deliberate choice behind the entry, merged and de-duplicated from N9's recovery of the project files and session transcripts and from each night agent's build/N*/decisions.json. Fields: id, category, decision, why, evidence, alternative_rejected, shows_up_in, strength, plus plain (one-or-two-sentence version for the site), decided_by, when, status, top10 (rank group in the 'ten choices' list), sources_merged and agent_records (provenance).

top10.title: No AI in the product, on purpose
top10.text: AI helped one person audit 1.5 million requests and draft the closure classes; the product itself is plain SQL with template text. The city's AI policy (ITSA #2026-001, July 2026) bars staff from any AI tool ITSA has not approved, so this is something the city can run without that approval.

top10.title: Graded against the city's own promise
top10.text: Every 311 request carries the date the city itself promises (3 days for a streetlight, 5 for a tow, usually 14 for a vacant lot). We grade against that, not against a target we picked.

top10.title: 'Closed' read in the city's own words, in a table anyone can overrule
top10.text: We separate 'work completed' from 'referred', 'scheduled' and 'work order created' using the exact closing text, and publish every mapping so the city can disagree line by line. We show the headline two ways so it does not rest on one debatable class.

top10.title: Fairness measured like for like, including against our own headlines
top10.text: Our first headline compared a quick desk referral in the southwest with field work in the north. We now compare only the same request type closed with the same words, from residents, before and after the tornado, against thresholds fixed in advance. What survives is the wait for the city's first act (a towed car is tagged in 12 days in the southwest and 37 in the north, against a promise of 5); since the May 2025 tornado, finished work mostly shows no gap; and the streetlight comparison we planned to lead with failed the test, so it was dropped.

top10.title: Blocks, not addresses; no personal data
top10.text: Every public page shows blocks, never a house or lot, by Jack's ruling. No field about a person enters the pipeline, and no request, work-order or parcel id appears in public. A private note about exposed data is being raised with the city through the hackathon organiser.

top10.title: We decline to watch people
top10.text: We do not try to identify dumping suspects (the city's surveillance ordinance requires aldermanic approval for that, and cameras elsewhere catch few), and requests about people rather than places (encampments, homeless calls, welfare checks, discrimination complaints) are never shown below ward level.

top10.title: Every record checked against a second record
top10.text: Before calling the forestry billing ledger a cut record we checked it against CityStat's own mowing count (7,545 lots against 7,099), and because it posts in weekly batches we count weeks, not days.

top10.title: Every number shows how we know it, and what failed is shown too
top10.text: Each figure carries its sources, joins and corrections behind a 'How we know' link, and the site lists what we tested that did not hold.

top10.title: Runs on what the city already has
top10.text: Public files the city already publishes, fetched by the weekly job only where the city's robots file allows, with free tools and no key, by staff it already employs. Under the city's IT rules that is an enhancement, not a procurement, and what we hand over is SQL and definitions, not a hosted app.

top10.title: We say what it cannot do
top10.text: Data does not cut grass: crews and money are the city's binding constraints. We do not claim residents give up (we tested and found no sign of it within a year), we call repeat reports 'came back' rather than false closures, we say 'no cut billed in the ledger' rather than 'never mowed', and we say cancelled tree requests turn up in Forestry's work orders 'five times as often', not 'mostly converted'.

decisions.decision: Codes about people rather than places are never shown below ward level: homeless calls, tent encampments, welfare checks, and requests in the Discrimination, Legal Claims and Courts groups or routed to Human Services, Civil Rights or the police (SLMPD). Requests routed to SLMPD are also dropped row by row from the Monday list.
decisions.why: COMMON: no encampment or homeless-call points, ever. The same reasoning covers welfare checks and discrimination complaints. N8 finding 14: 28 'SLMPD Referral' rows reached the public Monday list; police matters are out of scope (README, BUILD-SPEC).
decisions.alternative_rejected: Showing them at block level like other codes.
shows_up_in: excluded from Monday list, receipts, dumping sites.
decisions.plain: Requests about people rather than places (homeless calls, encampments, welfare checks, discrimination and legal complaints, anything routed to Human Services or Civil Rights) are never shown below ward level, and a code is judged sensitive by its usual routing so that a few odd rows do not hide a whole service.

decisions.decision: No request, work-order or parcel ids in anything under build/out/. Sample receipts are numbered R001-R200; the key to request ids is build/N1/private/receipts_key.json. The Monday list is published without ids; the copy with ids (what a division would work from) is build/N1/private/monday_list_with_ids.csv. Hero receipts stay in build/N1/private/receipts_heroes.json.
decisions.why: COMMON correction 10 (N5's call, adopted 14 Oct, Jack to confirm): each id leads straight to an exact address in the city's own 311 file, undoing block-level rounding. privacy_check.py now fails the run if an id field, or any seven-digit number that equals a request id, appears in an N1 export.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Publishing request ids beside block-level addresses (makes the receipt search and the Monday list work out of the box, but points at exact properties).
decisions.status: in force tonight (COMMON correction 10); Jack to confirm in the morning
decisions.plain: No request, work-order or parcel id appears anywhere public: sample receipts are numbered R001-R200, the Monday list is published without ids, and the build fails if an id slips into an export, because each id leads straight back to an exact address in the city's own files and would undo block-level rounding. The receipt search can still be shown working on an id a visitor types. N5 proposed it; the orchestrator adopted it for tonight; Jack confirms.

decisions.decision: Routing values (SUBMITTO) used fewer than 20 times are pooled as 'Other (pooled)'; resolution text used fewer than 5 times in the whole file is shown as '[uncommon free text withheld]'; e-mail addresses are removed from any text. The raw columns stay in the database.
decisions.why: Observed: three SUBMITTO values are people's names (used 1 to 3 times each), and one canned resolution carries a staff e-mail (18 requests). Rare free text can name people. Orchestrator instruction, 14 Oct.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Publishing SUBMITTO and resolution text verbatim; hand-listing the names (would miss next week's).
decisions.plain: We never publish the raw routing field or rare closing text, and strip e-mail addresses, because a few routing values are people's names and one canned closing text carries a staff e-mail. Rare values are pooled; the raw columns stay in the local database.

decisions.decision: The page reads only site/data/*.json, written by scripts/night/N6/bridge.py; it never fetches build/ directly.
decisions.why: The agents' own files carry fields the public page must never show (N5's first heroes.json had a parcel id, handle, coordinates and house-number address; N1's receipts carried request ids). Copying only contract fields, then scanning, means nothing finer than a block reaches site/ (COMMON 'Public outputs: block level'; correction 10).
decisions.alternative_rejected: Serving the repository root and reading build/out/*.json and build/N*/*.json in the browser with JavaScript adapters.
decisions.plain: The site reads only its own data folder, written by a bridge script that copies contract fields and nothing else, never the agents' build files, because those files carry fields a public page must not show (an early hero file had a parcel id, coordinates and a house-number address).

decisions.decision: scripts/night/N6/privacy_scan.py checks every text file under site/ for request and work-order ids (exact match against N1's 1,454,222 request ids and 4,525 work orders), parcel-like ids, coordinates, e-mail addresses and house-number addresses. It found and removed the lead lot's exact address, which had been used as an example in DATA-CONTRACT.md.
decisions.why: The block-level rule binds every public output, including documentation that ships inside site/.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Relying on the bridge's scrubbing alone.
decisions.plain: A privacy scan checks every file the site ships for request and work-order ids, parcel-like ids, coordinates, e-mail and house-number addresses; it caught and removed the lead lot's exact address from a documentation example.

decisions.decision: Every public output shows locations at block level (house number rounded down to the hundred block), never a house or lot address, including the hero lot in the video.
decisions.why: Jack's ruling, about 11:50 p.m. on 13 Oct, after the orchestrator proposed an exception for city-owned (land bank) lots: he preferred blocks to a specific house everywhere. The rule predates the ruling (T-COMMON: 'Report nothing below block level on any public-facing output'). Nobody private can be pinpointed, and the claim does not need more precision than a block.
evidence: prompts/night-v2/COMMON.md (Rules: 'Public outputs: block level or coarser, including the hero examples')
context/NIGHT-PLAN.md decision 4 (default was parcel level for LRA lots)
session transcript 1bc71fad, 13 Oct about 11:43-11:50 p.m. (proposal, Jack's reply, ruling recorded)
decisions.alternative_rejected: Parcel-level display for land-bank (LRA) lots only, proposed as the default in NIGHT-PLAN decision 4 because no private owner is exposed; and address-level display everywhere.
shows_up_in: site: receipt, Monday list, dumping page
decisions.plain: We show blocks, not addresses, everywhere, including the land-bank lot in the opening shot, because no resident or owner should be findable from our pages and no claim we make needs more precision than a block. Jack chose this over an exception for city-owned lots.

decisions.decision: No personal fields enter the pipeline: fields about people (owners, staff, contacts) are dropped from every file when it is loaded, not when pages are drawn. The 311 file itself has no requester identity.
decisions.why: The entry's argument is about trust, and the demo must show no personal data (firm requirement F3; tree leaf 4.2). The data audit observed that the 311 file carries no requester identity, while some other files the pipeline reads carry fields about people (observed).
evidence: research/data-audit.md section 2 (CSB: 'No requester identity in the file')
decisions.alternative_rejected: Load the raw files whole and filter at display time.
decisions.plain: We drop every field about people (owners, staff, contacts) when the files are loaded, not when pages are drawn, so no personal field ever reaches an output. The 311 file itself records no one's identity.

decisions.decision: Aerial images frame the whole block with no marker on the lot; any parcel-level image or address is kept in build/N5/private/ for Jack only.
decisions.why: Follows from the block-level ruling: an image centred on a lot with a pin is an address by other means.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Centre the image on the hero lot with a marker, as a receipt would naturally do.
decisions.plain: Aerial images frame the whole block with no pin on the lot, because a picture centred on one lot is an address by other means.

decisions.decision: Request-level rows stay in the local database; public exports are aggregated to type x ward x quarter, plus block-level receipts for a curated sample.
decisions.why: Address-level joins are needed to compute (request to parcel to ledger cut), but nothing below block level may leave the build.
evidence: context/BUILD-SPEC.md (Data layer: 'request level stays in the database')
decisions.alternative_rejected: Publish the joined request-level table so others can re-run the analysis.
decisions.plain: Request-level rows stay in the local database and only aggregates and block-level receipts are exported, because the joins need addresses but the public does not.

decisions.why: Block-level rounding is the rule for every public output (Jack's ruling). The lot is city-owned, so no private owner is exposed and the orchestrator judged it acceptable under the rule, but the combination undoes the rounding in practice; Jack asked for blocks rather than a specific property, so it is his call.

decisions.plain: Open for Jack: the lead receipt shows the land-bank lot's block alongside details (acquisition year, a neighbouring lot's block) that together point to one parcel. It is city-owned, so no private owner is exposed, but it narrows the block-level rule he set.

evidence: session transcript 81405052, 13 Oct about 7:30-7:35 p.m. (worker reports)
decisions.alternative_rejected: Download everything keyless and sort it out later.
decisions.plain: During the data audit we skipped layers whose only extra content was personal, and used no keys, sign-ins or forms.

decisions.decision: Decline the 'identify and track down perpetrators' half of Ben's illegal-dumping problem set, and say so on the page; deliver repeat sites at block level and what happened after each report instead.
decisions.why: Identifying people is surveillance under tree branch 7.2 and any city use of surveillance technology needs the Board of Aldermen after a public hearing (Ordinance 71842, effective 6 May 2024, observed). Cameras catch few offenders where tried: Oakland cited 13% of 457 recorded incidents (reported, KGO-TV, 5 Aug 2024). The 311 file already codes enforcement outcomes ('summons issued' 458, 'not enough evidence' 298, 'cleared by arrest' 267, observed), so the useful half needs no new watching.
decisions.alternative_rejected: A perpetrator-identification or camera-placement tool, which is what the problem set asks for first.
shows_up_in: site: illegal dumping page (the declining paragraph)
decisions.plain: We decline the 'track down perpetrators' half of the dumping challenge and say so on the page, because identifying people needs the Board of Aldermen's approval under the city's surveillance ordinance and cameras elsewhere catch few offenders (Oakland cited 13% of incidents). We show repeat sites and what happened after each report instead.

decisions.decision: No map, list or count by location of 'Tent Encampment' or 'Homeless Call' requests, ever; Ben's unhoused problem set is not built.
decisions.why: Both codes exist in the 311 file (262 and 219 rows in 2025-26, observed), so a location tool could be made, but it would map where people sleep (tree branch 7.2, exposure). The other half of the ask, shelter-bed availability, has no data to show (fails F3).
evidence: research/synthesis-notes.md 'Checks after Ben's document' (codes and counts)
prompts/night-v2/COMMON.md (Rules: 'No encampment or homeless-call points, ever')
decisions.alternative_rejected: A location and outreach-targeting tool for Ben's problem set 2 built from those 311 codes.
shows_up_in: site: register (shelter row says no record exists)
README: what it does not fix
decisions.plain: We never map or count encampment or homeless-call requests by place, because a map of where people sleep is surveillance, not a service; the shelter-bed question has no data behind it, and the register says so.

decisions.decision: Raise exposed data with the city privately, through the hackathon organiser, and describe it nowhere in public. The only public line: 'A private note about exposed data is being raised with the city through the hackathon organiser.'
decisions.why: Describing what is exposed, even in general terms, would point others at it before the city can act; staying silent would leave it exposed. A private note is a good-faith act the office can act on. Only metadata and counts were ever read. The note is drafted and is Jack's to send; it had not been sent as of 14 Oct about 01:00, so no public text may say it was sent.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Describe the exposure in the public write-up, site or video; or say nothing to the city.
decisions.when: 13 Oct about 10:55 p.m.; public wording fixed 14 Oct about 01:05
decisions.status: drafted, NOT sent; Jack's to send, then update the one public line
decisions.plain: A private note about exposed data is being raised with the city through the hackathon organiser. We describe it nowhere in public, because a description would point others at it before the city can act.

decisions.decision: Personal data we came across in city-hosted data while auditing it is not used in any form, not even aggregated or anonymised.
decisions.why: Jack asked whether such data could be used the way a responsible company uses anonymised data, to show that unmet requests change how households engage. The synthesis rejected it: the city's AI policy says 'Do not input sensitive or regulated data', any such use falls under the surveillance ordinance, the entry's argument is trust, and every finding is already aggregate and address-free, so the data is also unnecessary.
evidence: ITSA IT Policy #2026-001, https://www.stlouis-mo.gov/government/departments/information-technology/documents/upload/Artificial-Intelligence-Policy-2.pdf (observed by research thread C)
decisions.alternative_rejected: Anonymised, aggregate use of that data to link service failures to residents.
decisions.plain: Personal data we came across while auditing city-hosted data is not used here in any form, not even aggregated, because the city's AI policy forbids feeding in sensitive data, its surveillance ordinance would govern such use, and every finding we make is already aggregate.

decisions.decision: Election, survey and demographic material is used only as framing, never as evidence that service failures cause anything about residents or votes; no request is linked to a person or household attribute.
decisions.why: Nothing in the data can support causation about votes or demographic harm, and individual-level linkage would need personal data the entry refuses to use. The 2025 race being reported as decided on basic services, and the city's own line that how well CSB works 'is directly tied to trust', are context only.
evidence: context/HANDOFF-2.md section 1 ('The electorate material is framing only')
decisions.alternative_rejected: A heat map tying unmet requests to older residents or to turnout, which Jack floated as a way to show impact.
decisions.plain: We use election and survey material only as context, because nothing in the data can show that service failures change votes or drive particular groups away.

decisions.decision: Drop the tornado-repair prioritisation variant.
decisions.why: Ranking households for aid from outside on partial data fails the personal-data gate and the harm branch: a wrong ranking lands on a household.
decisions.alternative_rejected: A ranked list of tornado-repair applicants.
decisions.plain: We dropped ranking tornado-repair applicants, because a wrong ranking from outside, on partial data, lands on a household.

decisions.decision: Build only on files the city already publishes and on free tools (Python, DuckDB), so that running it needs no new licence, no purchase and no new hire.
decisions.why: The city's IT governance page routes a request that 'uses only existing software licenses and hardware' and can be done by existing staff to an ITSA team as an enhancement, not to the IT Project Governance Committee; requiring procurement triggers committee review whatever the price (observed). The research thread's judgement: the shortest documented route is a department sponsor plus the CityStat team on data and licences the city already holds (inferred).
evidence: research/parts/E-stl-city-it.md (Project Request Form, 'No, uses only existing software licenses and hardware')
decisions.alternative_rejected: A tool on a commercial platform or paid API, which would make it a procured 'strategic project'.
shows_up_in: README: how the city would run it
decisions.plain: We built only on files the city already publishes and on free tools, because the city's IT rules send work that 'uses only existing software licenses and hardware' to an ITSA team as an enhancement, while anything needing procurement goes to a committee.

decisions.decision: AI is the method, not the product: AI helped one person audit the files and draft the closure-text classes, but the product itself runs no AI. It is plain SQL, Python and DuckDB with template text.
decisions.why: ITSA IT Policy #2026-001 (23 Jul 2026, observed) prohibits 'Use of any AI tool that has not been approved by ITSA'; approval needs a business case, costs, a procurement method, a data-retention plan and staff AI training, and AI output may not be published without human verification. A product with no model in it can be run by the city without that approval, and a person can check every output.
evidence: session transcript 1bc71fad, about 11:50 p.m. (Jack: a built-out system that does not rely on AI to be maintained)
decisions.alternative_rejected: An AI chatbot, summariser or classifier running inside the product (the obvious move at a 'Civic AI' hackathon), which would need ITSA approval before any staff use.
decisions.plain: We used AI to audit the files, but the product runs none: it is plain SQL with template text. The city's AI policy (ITSA #2026-001) bars staff from using any AI tool ITSA has not approved, so an AI-free product is one the city can run without that approval.

decisions.decision: No new staff is a firm requirement: the users are people the city already employs (the CityStat programme manager and research analyst, ITSA's analysts), and the pipeline replaces hand assembly rather than adding work.
decisions.why: Jack: 'having to hire ppl is a huge downside/barrier to implementation.' The city's capacity is thin: 20.7% of 6,420 budgeted positions vacant; Forestry at about 60% of seasonal mowing staff (reported).
decisions.alternative_rejected: A programme or tool that needs a new post, volunteers with no base, or contract labour.
decisions.plain: Nothing here needs a new hire: the users already exist (the CityStat team and ITSA's analysts) and the job replaces work they now do by hand.

decisions.decision: What the city adopts is the SQL and the definitions, not our hosting: deliver files the CityStat team could run without our code or our servers.
decisions.why: Precedents show adoption follows output that drops into a routine the city already runs, using data it already holds (research E). The project's lesson: 'One owner, one ask: the city adopts links into its own routine, not apps.'
decisions.alternative_rejected: A hosted app the city would have to procure, host or depend on us to run.
shows_up_in: README: how the city would run it
decisions.plain: What we hand over is SQL and definitions the CityStat team can run themselves, not an app on our servers, because cities adopt outputs that drop into routines they already run.

decisions.decision: Make the ask 'let the CityStat team run it weekly for a quarter' (B: 'from the first cut next spring').
decisions.why: A concrete, reversible, low-cost ask that one office can approve; the COO's own framing is CityStat functions that 'continue to grow' (research/mayors-office-voice.md 5.1).
decisions.alternative_rejected: 'Adopt DoneStat', or a hosting request.
decisions.status: drafted; Jack decides the words of the ask
decisions.plain: The ask is small and reversible: let the CityStat team run it weekly for one quarter, a request one office can approve.

decisions.decision: Running cost is effectively zero (free tools, public files, a weekly job), comfortably under the $2,500 per-transaction line below which no bids are needed.
decisions.why: Purchases up to $2,500 need no bids or advertising since March 2026 (observed); cost questions in the city's templates are about staff hours and recurring cost (observed).
decisions.alternative_rejected: Paid imagery, a hosted database or a SaaS dashboard.
decisions.plain: It costs nothing to run beyond staff time, well under the $2,500 line below which the city needs no bids.

decisions.decision: Release the code openly under the MIT licence, deployable as built.
decisions.why: Mike at the kickoff named 'open source and already built, that they can deploy' as 'even better' (observed in the transcript excerpt); this became weighed item W9.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Keep the code private and show only the demo.
decisions.status: provisional: public hosting is Jack's call
decisions.plain: The code is meant to be released under the MIT licence, because the organisers said open-source and already-built is what the city can deploy. Public hosting is Jack's call.

decisions.decision: Send four questions through the organiser before claiming more: does Cityworks update the request when its work order closes; is GeoSTL's satellite mowing work in use; what denominator CityStat's on-time charts use; is the tree backlog limited by crews or by the order of work.
decisions.why: Each answer could change the pitch: if Cityworks already propagates completion, the entry becomes 'publish it' (cheaper, not wrong); if GeoSTL delivers, mowing becomes 'the ledger they are not using'.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Assume the answers and build on the assumption.
decisions.plain: We wrote down the four questions that could change the pitch (does Cityworks already close the loop? is GeoSTL's mowing work live? what is CityStat's denominator? crews or ordering?) instead of assuming the answers.

decisions.decision: Present the register as the city's roadmap: 4 of 25 services can be joined to a completion record on public files today; of the other 21, the register names Cityworks work orders for 5 (trees, tree planting, potholes, cave-ins, street lights), and the rest need other division records (tow lot, truck GPS, Building Division, CEMA, Human Services, the 50/50 programme).
decisions.why: That turns the register from a list of gaps into a list of specific records to connect, without new software (N2's register; N8 corrected an earlier 'most' to 5 of 21).
decisions.alternative_rejected: Present the register as a list of failings.
decisions.plain: The register doubles as a roadmap: four of 25 services can be checked on public files today; for five more (trees, tree planting, potholes, cave-ins, street lights) the missing record is the city's own work orders, and the rest need other division records.

decisions.decision: NAIP 2024 is the public image for every hero (ten block frames, *_block_naip2024.png); MSDIS 2022/2024/2025 frames are marked not cleared.

NAIP 2024 metadata (meta/naip2024_mo510.xml, USDA FPAC-BC-GEO) carries only 'requires a general understanding of GIS'; NAIP is a USDA product, public domain (reported). NAIP at 0.3 m is legible at block scale: streets, houses, lots, tree crowns and even mowing patterns show.
