decisions.decision: Nothing is published or pushed overnight: the baseline commit is local only, and public hosting (for example GitHub Pages) waits for Jack.
decisions.why: Hosting is outward-facing, and outward-facing actions are Jack's (AGENTS.md boundaries). N8 also found the repository cannot be published as it stands (private folders not ignored; the baseline commit holds request and parcel ids), so publication needs a fresh repository with one clean commit.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Publish the prototype overnight so it is ready when he wakes.
decisions.plain: Nothing was published or pushed overnight, because anything outward-facing is Jack's to do.

decisions.decision: The one AI-assisted step, classing the city's closing text, is delivered as a reviewable rule table (problem code, exact closing text, class, count, rule or judgement) that SQL applies; a person can read and overrule every line.
decisions.why: Keeps the product AI-free at runtime and is how the policy's 'treat AI output as a draft' clause is met. It also lets the CityStat team disagree with a class without touching code. N2's Python and SQL versions agree on all 2,992 type-and-text pairs, and N3's independently written rules agree with N2 on 98.4% of closures (observed); no person has reviewed the table yet.
evidence: build/N2/figures.json notes ('drafted by an AI model and open for review')
decisions.alternative_rejected: Classify closures with a model at run time, or by opaque keyword rules nobody reviews.
decisions.status: in force; open to review, not yet reviewed by a person (ten distinct texts carry about 60% of hand-off closures; about 40 type-and-text pairs for a per-type review, N8)
decisions.plain: The one AI-assisted step, sorting the city's closing words into 'done', 'handed off' and so on, ships as a table open to review, which a person can read and overrule line by line, so nothing in the product depends on a model. A second agent's independent rules agree on 98.4% of closures; no person has reviewed it yet.

decisions.decision: Read 'closed' through the city's own closing words: every closing text is classed as done, handed off (scheduled, referred, added to rotation, tagged, 'will be', sent elsewhere), converted (work order created), no action, other, or blank.
decisions.why: Closed requests include referrals and hand-offs, not only finished work: a cave-in shows Closed with 'Referred to street maintenance for repair work to be scheduled'; the towing page itself says 'Closed' does not necessarily mean towed (observed). So a closed status, and the time it took to reach it, does not by itself say the work was done.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Treat STATUS = CLOSED as done, which is what time-to-close (and CityStat) implicitly does.
decisions.plain: We read 'closed' through the city's own closing words and separate 'work completed' from 'referred', 'scheduled' and 'work order created', because the 311 system closes a request when a job is handed off, not when it is done.

decisions.decision: Test every claim against an independent record before making it, and run the test that could falsify it; record the result either way.
decisions.why: The project's working rule since the synthesis: ledger against CityStat; cancellations against work orders; re-filing after a cut against no cut; the exit test. Two tests came back negative and are kept (no exit; status text does not drive re-filing).
decisions.alternative_rejected: Report findings from one file at a time.
shows_up_in: site: 'What we tested that did not hold'
decisions.plain: We test each claim against a second, independent record and run the test that could prove it wrong, and we keep the result either way.

decisions.decision: Treat forestry-ledger dates as precise to the week, not the day, and say so beside every figure that uses them.
decisions.why: Postings are batched: 8,507 of the 2026 rows carry a Sunday date and 2,608 carry 23 April (observed). SERVICEDATE is a posting date. Any figure counted in days (the 35% cut within 30 days) carries that caveat; if challenged, lead with 'no cut billed all season' (about one in five vacant-lot requests closed 'on schedule to be cut': 21.4% of 729; a quarter if 'added to rotation' closures are included, N8).
decisions.alternative_rejected: Read the ledger as a day-level operations log.
decisions.plain: We read the forestry ledger's dates to the week, not the day, because it posts in weekly batches (8,507 of 2026's rows are dated a Sunday).

decisions.decision: Compare wards like for like: same request type, same closing class (done-class closures), resident channels, and also share done by the city's promised date counting open and cancelled requests as not done.
decisions.why: Raw time-to-close mixes types and closing practice. Cave-ins in wards 1-5 close in a median 1.1 days mostly because their closures read 'referred ... to be scheduled' (median 0.8 days); 'work completed' takes 8.3 days there against 23.1 in wards 10-14 (observed, distinct requests, N3/N5; 9.6 vs 25.1 on rows), but only 35 such repairs are recorded in wards 1-5, so the repair gap is unproven and repair dates for referred cave-ins are in no public file; the referral step itself takes 0.8 against 41.7 days. Across all services, type mix and closing words explain only 12% of CityStat's ward 1 vs ward 10 gap (N3). N3 applied the rule to 79 types; the comparisons that survive are about first steps (towing tagged, cave-in referral, building-code notices).
decisions.alternative_rejected: Raw median days to close by ward, the measure behind the earlier headline and CityStat's own ward chart.
decisions.plain: We compare wards on the same request type closed with the same words, because raw closing times mix different steps. For cave-ins the gap sits in the referral step itself (0.8 against 41.7 days), and when a referred cave-in is repaired is in no public file; across all services, type mix and closing words explain only 12% of the city's ward 1 versus ward 10 gap, so most of it is the same request, closed with the same words, later.

decisions.decision: Grade every request against the promise date the city itself sets on it (PRJCOMPLETEDATE), not against CityStat's goals or our own targets.
decisions.why: The field is a fixed offset per request type (single light out 3 days, cave-ins 3, towing 5, residential potholes 8, alley potholes 16, illegal dumping 10, debris 3, tree inspection 14, weeds on a vacant lot 14, weeds at a vacant building mostly 90) and is filled on about 98% of rows (observed, 13 Oct about 11:30 p.m.; N1: 97.9% of 2024-26 requests, offsets identical). It is the city's own promise, so nobody can say we picked the bar; CityStat's goals rest on unpublished denominators and differ from the city's own due dates for 3 of 9 services (alley potholes 16 vs 17 days; whole-block lights 2 days vs 24 hours; critical signs 3 days vs 48 hours; observed, N4). Caveat: for vacant-lot weeds the offset is 14 days on some 2026 requests and 90 on others, so the date is shown as given (N5).
evidence: session transcript 1bc71fad, about 11:28-11:37 p.m. (field noticed while spot-checking)
decisions.alternative_rejected: Grade against CityStat's published goals (whose denominators are unpublished) or our own guess at a reasonable time.
shows_up_in: site: receipt ('the city's own promised date was ...')
decisions.plain: We grade every request against the date the city itself promises on it (the PRJCOMPLETEDATE field: 3 days for a streetlight, 5 for a tow, usually 14 for a vacant lot), because then nobody can say we chose the bar.

decisions.decision: Fairness comparisons use resident-filed requests only (web, phone, email, chat, Twitter, letter); staff-entered requests (NSO) are excluded and 'indeterminate' is reported separately.
decisions.why: Staff-entered requests are 18-24% of the total in wards 10-14, so part of the north-side count is inspectors' own work, which follows a different clock (observed by the synthesis session).
decisions.alternative_rejected: All channels together, which mixes inspectors' self-generated work into residents' waits.
decisions.plain: Fairness comparisons count only requests residents filed themselves, because staff-entered requests are a fifth or more of the north-side total and follow inspectors' own schedules.

decisions.decision: Before using the billing ledger as the city's cut record, check it against an independent count: parcels with a cut posted 6 April-26 May 2026 against CityStat's first mowing rotation.
decisions.why: 7,545 parcels in the ledger against CityStat's '7,099 of 12,171' for the same rotation (observed): the ledger matches at rotation level and is probably CityStat's source. A billing charge is not an operations log, so the check had to be made before the claim.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Assume the ledger is a cut record because its rows look like one.
decisions.plain: Before calling the billing ledger a cut record, we checked it against CityStat's own mowing count for the same weeks: 7,545 lots against 7,099. It holds at that level.

decisions.decision: Split the ward gap with an exact two-level Kitagawa decomposition of the mean: type mix, then closing-class shares within type, then speed within the same type and class. Check with median reweighting and with days capped at 90.
decisions.why: CityStat's metric is a mean, which splits exactly with no residual and can be shown as arithmetic. The median and capped versions give the same answer (speed within type and class is 99-148% of the gap).
decisions.alternative_rejected: Regression with ward dummies (harder to explain to an analyst; same conclusion expected).
decisions.plain: We split the ward 1 versus ward 10 gap with an exact, checkable decomposition (type mix, closing words, then speed within the same type and words), because the city's chart uses a mean, which splits with no remainder. The answer was not what we expected: mix and closing words explain about 12% of it.

decisions.decision: Rest the mowing and hero-lot claims on the 2026 season, not 2025.
decisions.why: The 2025 ledger is thin (8,780 parcels cut against 17,295 in 2024 and 16,118 in 2026; observed, N5), consistent with crews moved to tornado debris, so 'no cut in 2025' is weak evidence.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Use two seasons to show persistence.
decisions.plain: The mowing claims rest on 2026, because the 2025 ledger is thin (crews went to tornado debris) and 'no cut in 2025' proves little.

decisions.decision: Join requests to parcels by normalised address text against the MSD parcel attribute file (PID equals the city's ParcelId), with owner names dropped, and always report the match rate; below 80% for weed requests is a knock-out.
decisions.why: The 311 file has addresses and coordinates but no parcel id; the ledger has parcel ids but no addresses. MSD's file bridges them for 134,919 city parcels (observed). Matches ran 85% for 2026 weed requests in the synthesis check (3,962 of 4,658); N1's tested normaliser and number-range step reach 90.1% (vacant lots, 2,387 of 2,649) and 93.3% (vacant buildings) for 2025-26, above the 80% knock-out (observed).
decisions.alternative_rejected: Spatial join on SRX/SRY to parcel polygons (needs the parcel shapefile with owner fields), or no join.
decisions.plain: We link a 311 address to a parcel through MSD's parcel address file and always report how many matched (90% of vacant-lot weed requests, 93% of vacant-building ones), because the 311 file has no parcel id and the ledger has no address.

decisions.decision: Publish a conservative version of the hand-off headline that counts enforcement notices to owners (notice of violation, already under notice, warning, ticket, summons) as neither hand-off nor done.
decisions.why: A notice is a real action but not the fix; showing both versions (35.2% and 25.2% of 2025-26 closures, observed by N2) stops the headline resting on a contestable class.
decisions.alternative_rejected: One headline figure that counts notices as hand-offs without saying so.
decisions.plain: We show the hand-off share two ways (35.2%, and 25.2% if enforcement notices count as neither), so the headline does not hang on one debatable class.

decisions.decision: Three firm gates only (no new staff; residents measurably affected; demo on real data we hold); everything else (an existing tool, data not yet collected, no owning department, several approvers, cost, being on Ben's list) is weighed with evidence and never used alone to drop an idea.
decisions.why: Jack rejected the earlier draft's seven knock-outs as rigid: an excellent idea should not die because a poor tool exists or the data is elsewhere.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Seven knock-out criteria from the previous session's draft.
decisions.plain: Only three things could rule an idea out (needing new staff, no measurable effect on residents, no real data); everything else was weighed with evidence, because Jack judged seven knock-outs too rigid.

decisions.decision: An independent agent (N8) recomputes every on-screen figure from the raw files before reading the producing script, and scans for personal data, mock data and overclaims.
decisions.why: The people who built a number are the worst placed to see what is wrong with it; the check runs before the COO sees anything.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Trust each agent's own validation.
decisions.plain: A separate agent recomputes every on-screen number from the raw files before the COO sees it.

decisions.decision: Report medians, and alongside them a survival-style share done by the promised date that counts open requests as not done.
decisions.why: Closed-only medians understate a gap where more requests stay open: cave-ins open 40.6% in wards 10-14 against 17.6% in the southwest (observed). Medians resist the multi-year outliers in the file. Unresolved overnight: N1 and N3 count cancelled requests as not done in the promise measure, while N4's scoreboard drops them from the denominator (many are duplicates), so the citywide figures differ (N1 50.8% closed and 16.7% done by promise; N4 57.8% and 19.5%).
decisions.alternative_rejected: Mean days over closed requests only (CityStat's ward chart).
decisions.plain: We use medians and the share done by the promised date counting open requests as not done, because averages over closed requests hide the requests that never close.

decisions.decision: Measure residents' need by what they did (requests filed, waits, outcomes), not by news or forum attention or by what people say they would do.
decisions.why: Attention and need diverge: graffiti and heat are loud in the news and thin in the request file (observed, reports D and B). Requests are acts, 112,859 a year.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Rank problems by news and social-media volume.
decisions.plain: We measure need by what residents did (requests filed, waits) rather than by news coverage, because attention and need point at different problems.

decisions.decision: Before relaying any agent's headline to the others, the orchestrator recomputes it from the raw file.
decisions.why: N2's 35.2% hand-off share and N3's towing and cave-in medians matched exactly on recomputation; the towing promise share did not, and was held back. The full pipeline was also re-run to show figures reproduce (191 then 197 figures; only the build time changed).
decisions.alternative_rejected: Relay agents' figures as reported.
decisions.plain: Before any agent's number was passed on, the integrator recomputed it from the raw file; the one that did not match was held back.

decisions.decision: Reproduce CityStat's own figures from the public file before critiquing them, and report any gap as a finding about unpublished definitions with the question to ask.
decisions.why: The first quick recomputation (Q2 2026 potholes: major 48.6% of 494 against CityStat's 44.5% of 443; residential 81.1% against 90.6%; alley 82.9% against 98.2%) did not match, because it counted rows and used a different quarter state (observed). N4 then searched 1,440 definitions per metric: one shared rule (one row per request, closed requests only, quarter filed, close minus filed within goal) reproduces CityStat's published counts within 0.2% for 8 of 9 metrics (identical in 66 of 72 metric-quarters, never off by more than 4 requests; parks 2.1%) and its shares within 5 points in 76 of 81 metric-quarters (observed; figures n4_repro_counts_exact_C, n4_repro_metrics_within5pp_C). What does not reproduce is reported as questions: routing, the lights clock, and Q2 2026 pothole shares 4-6 points above the file.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Build a new scoreboard without showing whether the city's existing one can be recovered.
decisions.plain: We rebuilt CityStat's own figures from the public file before proposing anything new. One shared rule reproduces its published request counts within 0.2% for 8 of 9 metrics (identical in 66 of 72 metric-quarters, never off by more than 4 requests; parks 2.1%) and its percentages within 5 points in 76 of 81 quarters; where it does not match (routing, the lights clock, two Q2 pothole shares) we ask rather than accuse.

decisions.decision: A ward comparison is called robust only if it survives both done-class medians and share done by promise, has at least 100 requests on each side, and holds before and after the tornado; types need 300 or more resident requests since 16 May 2025 to be tested.
decisions.why: Small groups and single measures produced headlines that fell over (the cave-in and tree gaps). Fixed thresholds set before looking keep the shortlist from being cherry-picked.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Report whichever comparison shows the largest gap.
decisions.plain: A ward comparison counts as robust only if it holds on two measures, with at least 100 requests a side, before and after the tornado; we set those rules before looking.

decisions.decision: Split every ward comparison at the tornado (16 May 2025) and require a gap to hold on both sides before calling it robust.
decisions.why: The tornado moved crews and requests; a gap that exists only afterwards could be recovery work. The earlier check found the gaps predate it (for example towing, resident channels: 53.2 vs 31.2 days before, 36.9 vs 9.7 after; observed, rows).
decisions.alternative_rejected: Pool 2024-26, or use only the post-tornado period.
decisions.plain: We check every ward gap before and after the May 2025 tornado, so a gap caused by recovery work is not mistaken for a standing one.

decisions.decision: Lead with vacant lots, not vacant buildings, for the uncut-lot claim, and treat vacant-building figures as a lower bound.
decisions.why: Vacant-building lots are cut by contractors who may not be billed into the ledger: only 516 'Vacant Building' Grass Maint rows in 2026 (observed). So 11% cut within 30 days at vacant buildings is partly artefact; 35% at vacant lots (city crews) is the defensible figure.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Lead with the more dramatic vacant-building figure.
decisions.plain: We lead with vacant lots, not vacant buildings, because contractors cut vacant-building lots and may not be billed into the ledger, so those figures are a lower bound.

decisions.decision: The mowing retrospective flags rotation lots whose longest gap between cuts (or from the last cut to 30 Sep) exceeds 90 days; the 42-day count is reported beside it.
decisions.why: Observed: the median longest gap between consecutive cuts on 2026 rotation lots is 54 days, so the city's own cycle is about eight weeks; BUILD-SPEC's 42-day threshold flags 11,356 of 11,824 lots and says nothing. 90 days is about one and a half cycles, i.e. a missed rotation.
decisions.alternative_rejected: 42 days (flags 96% of lots).
decisions.plain: The mowing look-back flags lots that went more than 90 days without a billed cut (counting to 30 September), not 42 as first specified, because the city's own cycle runs about eight weeks (median longest gap 54 days) and a 42-day rule flags 96% of lots.

decisions.decision: For vacant-lot and vacant-building weed codes, the scoreboard adds a ledger column: share of parcel-matched requests with a cut recorded between filing and the city's promised date.
decisions.why: Their closures are almost all 'on schedule to be cut' or 'added to rotation' (hand-offs), so done-by-promise from the words alone is near zero and says nothing; the ledger is the city's own completion record.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Grading weeds by closure words only.
decisions.plain: Weed requests are graded by whether the ledger shows a cut by the promised date, not by their closing words, because almost every weed closure says 'on schedule to be cut', so the words alone say nothing.

decisions.decision: Class shares are shares of closures. Cancelled and open requests are reported beside them in the register, not folded in.
decisions.why: The brief asks what 'closed' means. Cancellation is its own large outcome for some services (city trees: 8,214 of 14,007 requests filed 2025-26 cancelled) and would distort a closure mix.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Counting CANCEL as a seventh closure class.
decisions.plain: Class shares are shares of closures; cancelled and open requests are reported beside them, because for some services cancellation is the main outcome (city tree requests: 8,214 of 14,007 cancelled) and folding it in would blur what 'closed' means.

decisions.decision: 'converted' only when a work order or crew work ticket is created (removal/trim work order created, Work order created, work ticket issued to crew). Programme queues (approved for next available planting, added to sewer lateral repair program, sidewalk programme, Major Capital Improvement Project) are handed_off:queued_program.
decisions.why: A work order is a record that can be joined and finished; a queue position is not published (50/50 sidewalk page: the wait 'depends on the amount of funds available in your ward').
decisions.alternative_rejected: Counting queues as conversions.
shows_up_in: class 'converted' (0.4% of closures, mostly tree inspections)
decisions.plain: 'Converted' means only that a work order or crew ticket was created; a place in a programme queue (such as the next available planting) is a hand-off, because a work order can be joined and finished and a queue position is not published.

decisions.decision: A service has an independent completion record only if a city file outside the 311 request holds dated work at an address that can be joined to the request. The Cityworks pothole layer does not count: its 1,500 sampled requests are the same REQUESTIDs with the same close times (time-zone offset).
decisions.why: The register is meant to show where 'done' can be checked, not where a second copy of the request exists.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Counting inventories (street lights, signals, sidewalks) or the request system's own copies as completion records.
decisions.plain: A service counts as having a completion record only if a city file outside 311 records dated work at an address we can join; the city's pothole work-order layer does not count because it is the same requests with the same close times.

decisions.decision: Report the cave-in referral gap (0.8 vs 41.7 days) as a process difference, not as like-for-like speed of work.
decisions.why: Per ward, referral time jumps from under 1.2 days (every ward 1-5) to over 15 days (every ward 6-14); the same 5|6 line appears in the towing and bad-condition investigation stamps, all Street Department types.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Calling the south 'fast' (its repair dates are not recorded) or the gap 'mix only' (the same words take 50 times longer).
decisions.plain: The cave-in referral gap (0.8 against 41.7 days) is reported as a difference in process at a line between wards 5 and 6, not as speed of repair, because referral time jumps at that line in every ward.

decisions.decision: Reproduce CityStat's ward chart as the mean (not median) days to close over STATUS=CLOSED requests, all channels and types, filed 1 Jan 2024-30 Jun 2026, ward as recorded in the file.
decisions.why: Of seven definitions tried this one fits best (mean absolute error 0.85 days across 14 wards; closed counts within 1.1%); a closed-by-10-July snapshot fits the closed counts best.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Resident-only (counts 29% low); counting cancellations as closures (closed counts 15% high); geocoding blank wards (not done; 2,561 blank-ward requests vs CityStat 726).
decisions.plain: We reproduced CityStat's ward chart as the mean days to close over closed requests, all channels, filed 1 Jan 2024 to 30 Jun 2026, which lands within 0.85 days per ward on average; that is the definition every comparison with the chart uses.

decisions.decision: Do not use DATEINVTDONE ('investigation done') as a like-for-like measure.
decisions.why: For Street Department types it is stamped within about a day in every ward 1-5 and after 7-64 days in wards 6-14, while towing tags in wards 1-5 still take 6-15 days, so in wards 1-5 it marks a desk step, not the visit. Forestry's stamp has its own line between wards 7 and 8.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Using the stamp as time to inspection (would show 25x gaps that are partly process).
decisions.plain: We do not use the file's 'investigation done' stamp to compare wards, because in wards 1-5 it marks a desk step within a day while tow tags there still take 6-15 days.

decisions.decision: The headline reproduction uses one shared definition C for every metric: one row per request number, closed requests only, quarter filed, on time = close date minus filed date <= goal. The best definition per metric (B) is reported beside it.
decisions.why: With 1,440 combinations and nine data points per metric, a per-metric best can fit noise. C alone lands within 5 points of CityStat in 76 of 81 metric-quarters, matches the counts within 0.2% on 8 of 9 metrics, and has a mean gap of 0.5-2.7 points on 7 of 9 metrics (build/N4/citystat_fit.json).
decisions.alternative_rejected: The per-metric best everywhere (also 76 of 81, but it brings overfit risk and gives the city several different rules to adopt).
decisions.plain: We reproduce every CityStat metric with one shared definition rather than the best fit per metric, because with 1,440 candidate definitions and nine quarters a per-metric best can fit noise, and the city needs one rule to adopt. The shared rule reproduces CityStat's published counts within 0.2% for 8 of 9 metrics (identical in 66 of 72 metric-quarters, never off by more than 4 requests; parks 2.1%).

decisions.decision: Report each Q3 2026 share with a floor: the value it reaches if every request still open on 13 Oct 2026 closes late.
decisions.why: A closed-only share can only fall as slow requests close. In past quarters, the share measured 12 days after the quarter ended overstated the final figure by up to 18.5 points for residential potholes and 27.1 points for alleys. Every Q3 request still open is already past goals of 12 days or less.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Publishing the closed-only figure alone, which repeats the pattern behind CityStat's preliminary Q2.
decisions.plain: Each Q3 share is shown with a floor (the value if every still-open request closes late), because a closed-only share can only fall and early readings have overstated the final by up to 27 points.

decisions.decision: In the scoreboard, leave cancelled requests out of the denominator (show the cancelled share beside it), and grade only requests whose due date had passed by 13 Oct 2026.
decisions.why: Many cancellations are duplicates, which are neither kept nor broken promises, and requests not yet due cannot be graded. The cancelled share is shown because for some types cancellation is the main outcome (Inspect City Tree 66%, Stump Removal 88%).
decisions.alternative_rejected: Counting cancellations as broken promises (overstates failure); counting requests not yet due (understates it).
decisions.status: in force for the scoreboard; differs from N1/N3's promise measure (see N9 report)
decisions.plain: The done scoreboard grades only requests already due and leaves cancelled requests out of the denominator, showing the cancelled share beside it, because many cancellations are duplicates. N1 and N3 count cancelled requests as not done, so the published measures differ: N4's scoreboard gives 57.8% closed and 19.5% done by the promised date; N1's citywide figures give 50.8% and 16.7%. The site should name which one it shows.

decisions.decision: Give the ward map a within-type version: each ward's average as if it had the citywide mix of request types (ward-type cells with fewer than five closures use the citywide average).
decisions.why: A ward with more slow request types looks slow even if each type is handled at the citywide pace. Adjusting does not narrow the Ward 1 vs Ward 10 gap (17.3 vs 32.2 days raw, 17.4 vs 32.2 adjusted), and north wards 11-14 get slower (Ward 13: 24.6 to 29.2), so type mix does not explain the gap.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Raw averages only (CityStat's view).
decisions.plain: We added a version of the ward map at the citywide mix of request types, which showed that mix does not explain the north-south gap (ward 10 stays at 32.2 days).

decisions.decision: Rejected lot candidates after validation (scripts/night/N5/03_lot_validate.py): a land-bank lot on the 700 block of Wilmington Av in Carondelet (not on Forestry's maintenance list and no cuts on its city block in 2026, so it may not be in the programme); a Walnut Park East lot (listed as 'Fenced & Locked or Paved Lot'); a Dutchtown lot (no 2026 cuts on its city block, last cut 2023); a Greater Ville lot on Dr Martin Luther King Dr (LRA offer accepted Sep 2024). A Lewis Place lot on Dr Martin Luther King Dr is a sound alternate (no 2026 cut; 15 other parcels on its city block billed in 2026) with fewer resident requests.
decisions.why: Each rejected case has a plausible innocent explanation in the city's own files; heroes must survive the obvious objection.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Ranking purely by days without a cut (build/N5/private/lot_candidates.csv).
decisions.plain: We rejected hero lots that had a plausible innocent explanation in the city's own files (not on the maintenance list, a fenced lot, a pending sale), because a hero must survive the obvious objection.

decisions.decision: The Monday brief's per-ward first-step table, its three lists and the week-on-week compliance table are computed by the bridge from N1's database views (promise, requests, receipt_base, request_wo_summary). Each is registered in build/N6/figures.json with a derivation.
decisions.why: N3 publishes ward-group medians, not per-ward medians for the towing tag; the brief needs per-ward rows and this week's lists. Ward-group medians from the database match N3 for towing (12.0 vs 36.9); for cave-in referrals they differ slightly (0.8 vs 41.1 here, 41.7 in N3, n 367/116 vs 361/115), because N1 fills blank wards from the polygons.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Leaving the brief to wait for further agent exports.
decisions.plain: The Monday brief's per-ward table and lists are computed from the pipeline's own database views and registered with derivations; its ward-group medians match N3 for towing exactly and differ slightly for cave-in referrals (41.1 against 41.7 days) because the pipeline fills blank wards from the ward map.

decisions.decision: Cut storyboard A's narration from 285 to 264 words (coordinator's limit 265), about 1:46 at 150 words a minute.
decisions.why: N8 finding 8: 285 words read as about 295 spoken words and filled the 1:56 budget with no pauses. Cuts: 'The city keeps a second record', 'And', the list of no-gap services (shown on screen), 'weekly' and 'the … team' in shot 6, 'on purpose' and 'let the CityStat team' in shot 7.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Keeping 285 words and reading faster.
decisions.plain: Cut storyboard A's narration from 285 to 264 words (coordinator's limit 265), about 1:46 at 150 words a minute. N8 finding 8: 285 words read as about 295 spoken words and filled the 1:56 budget with no pauses.

decisions.decision: Say 'since the tornado' wherever the script, README or progress report claims little or no ward gap where the work was done.
decisions.why: N8 finding 7: before 16 May 2025, finished residential potholes ran 22.3 vs 31.8 days and major-street potholes 15.2 vs 21.4; n3_no_gap_done_types_after is for requests filed after the tornado.
decisions.alternative_rejected: An unqualified 'no gap where the work is done'.
decisions.plain: Say 'since the tornado' wherever the script, README or progress report claims little or no ward gap where the work was done. N8 finding 7: before 16 May 2025, finished residential potholes ran 22.3 vs 31.8 days and major-street potholes 15.2 vs 21.4; n3_no_gap_done_types_after is for requests filed after the tornado.

decisions.decision: Exclude closures that read 'no forestry violations' from the uncut-lot measure.
decisions.why: Those lots are not expected to be cut; 85-86% of them have no 2026 cut, as expected (observed).
decisions.alternative_rejected: Count every closed weed request.
decisions.plain: Lots closed 'no forestry violations' are left out of the uncut-lot figures, because nobody expected them to be cut.

decisions.decision: Every overnight brief carries a working hypothesis, a knock-out condition that would kill it, and asks for an admission first.
decisions.why: A thread that can say 'my premise failed' early is worth more than one that reports around it (the one habit kept from the Stemma project).
decisions.alternative_rejected: Open-ended briefs that report whatever they find.
decisions.plain: Every overnight task started with a stated hypothesis and the result that would kill it, so a failed premise is reported first, not buried.

decisions.decision: 'Re-filed after closure' means another request with the same normalised address and problem code started after the closure time, within 14, 30, 60 or 90 days.
decisions.why: Address plus code is the only stable key in a file with no requester identity; starting the clock at closure separates 'came back' from duplicates filed while open.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Report B's measure (any two requests sharing address and code in 12 months, 23.7%), which counts duplicates filed while open.
decisions.plain: A request 'came back' if the same problem was reported at the same address after the closure, because address and problem are the only stable key in a file with no requester identity.

decisions.decision: Run `date` before writing any timestamp.
decisions.why: The synthesis thread overestimated the time by about five hours and had to correct every stamp; a research thread also wrote a status time ahead of the clock.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Estimate times from context.
decisions.plain: We check the clock before writing any time, after one session's timestamps drifted five hours.

decisions.decision: Split the night into separate agents (pipeline, closure classes, fairness, CityStat, heroes, then site, story, verification, record of choices) under one integrator, rather than one long thread.
decisions.why: One context cannot hold pipeline code, evidence reconciliation and the story without losing figures. Jack asked whether fewer, larger threads would be better; the answer was one integrator with fresh context plus parallel agents.
decisions.alternative_rejected: One thread with everything in context, or many threads with no integrator.
decisions.plain: The overnight work ran as parallel agents under one integrator, because one long context loses figures.

decisions.decision: Summaries use ward groups 1-5 (southwest and south), 6-9 (central) and 10-14 (north), always alongside per-ward figures.
decisions.why: Groups make small types readable; per-ward figures stop a group hiding a boundary. For cave-ins and towing the line ran between wards 1-5 and 6-14, not north against south (observed), which per-ward figures exposed.
decisions.alternative_rejected: North versus south only.
decisions.plain: We group wards (1-5, 6-9, 10-14) for readability but always show each ward too, because per-ward figures revealed that some lines run between wards 5 and 6, not north against south.

decisions.decision: Write figures to disk as they are read, and keep them exactly.
decisions.why: The Stemma project's synthesis step dropped about fifteen figures it had been given by relying on memory.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Hold figures in context and write at the end.
decisions.plain: Figures are written to disk as they are read, because a synthesis that relied on memory once dropped fifteen of them.

decisions.decision: channel_group = resident if any caller row is WEB, PHONE, EMAIL, CHAT, TWITTER or LETTER; else staff if any is NSO; else indeterminate if any is INDETERMINATE; else other.
decisions.why: A request with a resident caller was asked for by a resident even if staff also logged it. T-COMMON defines the channel groups; it does not say how to resolve an id with two caller types (13,677 ids, 0.9%).
decisions.alternative_rejected: First row's caller type (row order in the city file is arbitrary).
shows_up_in: promise, by_ward, ward like-for-like, scoreboard (resident-channel filters).
decisions.plain: When several people report the same request, it counts as resident-filed if any of them is a resident, because a resident asked for it even if staff also logged it.

decisions.decision: The run date ('as of') is the latest filing time in the 311 file (13 Oct 2026 00:33), not the clock time of the run.
decisions.why: Open-age and promise-passed figures must refer to the data's own date so a re-run on old files gives the same answer.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Wall-clock now().
decisions.plain: Every 'as of' date is the latest filing time in the 311 file, not the moment the job ran, so a re-run on the same files gives the same answer.

decisions.decision: Build into build/N1/stl.building.duckdb and swap it into build/stl.duckdb at the end.
decisions.why: Five other sessions read build/stl.duckdb tonight; a half-built file would give them wrong answers.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Writing build/stl.duckdb in place.
decisions.plain: The database is built to a temporary file and swapped in at the end, so nobody reads a half-built copy.

decisions.decision: Exports follow site/DATA-CONTRACT.md: every file carries the meta envelope; figures.json is keyed by id; receipts.json is a list with 'line' and contract-shaped timelines; monday_list.json has by_ward, by_type, rows and mowing; dumping_blocks.json and mowing_2026.json and run.json as named there. The pipeline's own scoreboard is scoreboard_n1.json so the site keeps N4's scoreboard.json.
decisions.why: N6's bridge takes build/out files first when they pass validation; matching the contract means no code change on the site. N4 owns the scoreboard definitions tonight (CityStat definition C).
decisions.alternative_rejected: Writing build/out/scoreboard.json in N1's own shape (would either fail validation or displace N4's numbers).
decisions.plain: Exports follow the site's data contract field for field, so the site reads the pipeline's files with no code change.

decisions.decision: The classes CSV covers every request type and closing text on closures of requests filed 1 Jan 2024 to 13 Oct 2026 (types under 100 closures flagged, not dropped). Measures and headlines use requests filed 1 Jan 2025 to 12 Oct 2026 that are CLOSED.
decisions.why: N1 needs a class for every closure; the brief asks for 2024-2026 strings and 2025-26 headlines. Filing date keeps cohorts comparable.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Only types with 100 or more closures (would leave N1 rows unclassed); closure-date cohorts.
decisions.plain: The class table covers every closing text from requests filed 2024-26 so every closure has a class; the headline figures use 2025-26 filings, so cohorts compare.

decisions.decision: Texts match after trimming, collapsing internal whitespace and lower-casing. The CSV shows trim(PUBLICRESOLUTION) with the city's internal spacing; blank closures appear as an empty string with class blank. One closing text contains a staff e-mail address; it is written out with the address removed and matched by its prefix.
decisions.why: 530 closures (2024-26, deduplicated) differ only by leading or trailing spaces; no staff fields in outputs (COMMON rules).
decisions.alternative_rejected: Exact raw-string joins (fail on spacing); publishing the raw text with the e-mail.
decisions.plain: Closing texts are matched after trimming spaces and ignoring case, because 530 closures differ only by stray spaces.

decisions.decision: Assign each request to the quarter it was filed, not the quarter it was closed.
decisions.why: Quarter of closure fits CityStat worse on every metric: best mean gaps are 1.97-21.7 points, against 0.46-3.76 for quarter filed (build/N4/definition_search.json). The margin is small only for whole-block lights (3.82 vs 3.76).
decisions.alternative_rejected: Quarter of closure.
decisions.plain: Requests are assigned to the quarter they were filed, not closed, because that is what reproduces CityStat.

decisions.decision: For the parks metric, use each request's own PRJCOMPLETEDATE as its goal.
decisions.why: CityStat says parks goals range from five to thirty days by type but does not list them. The city's due-date offsets for these parks types are 3 to 21 days (3, 7, 9, 10, 14, 16, 21). Graded against them, parks requests reproduce CityStat within 2.3 points on average, with 9 of 9 quarters within 5 and counts within 2%.
decisions.alternative_rejected: One flat goal for all parks requests.
decisions.plain: For parks requests we grade against each request's own promised date, because CityStat does not list its parks goals.

decisions.decision: Light pair = requests within half a day of each ward group's median (deduplicated), same intake channel, filed closest together in time.
decisions.why: Representative rather than extreme, and same season (both December 2025, both web).
decisions.alternative_rejected: The longest waits, or COMMON.md's medians with duplicate rows.
decisions.plain: Paired examples are chosen near each ward group's median, in the same season and channel, not at the extremes, so a single case is representative.

decisions.decision: Use the city's forestry billing ledger (forestry-service-records.csv, 2,252,031 rows) as its per-lot record of grass cuts: 'Grass Maint' and 'Weed-Grass' rows count as cuts.
decisions.why: In 2026 it holds 37,543 Grass Maint postings (about 31,500 distinct parcel-days: the ledger repeats some rows, N8) on 11,972 parcels, 7,425 of them land-bank lots (observed), while CityStat's manager said in August that per-lot mowing status 'we don't have that tracked in a system' (reported, First Alert 4, 14 Aug 2026). The data the city says it lacks is on its own open-data portal.
evidence: research/synthesis-notes.md 'Forestry service records' and correction note
decisions.alternative_rejected: Satellite imagery as the cut record, or no cut record (take the 311 'closed' at face value).
decisions.plain: We use the city's forestry billing ledger as its record of which lots were cut, because it holds dated cut charges on about 12,000 lots in 2026, while the city has said per-lot mowing is not tracked in a system.

decisions.decision: Say plainly, once, that no city dataset states a licence, rather than implying one.
decisions.why: None of the city's 72 catalogued datasets carries a licence value in data.json, and no export, API or ArcGIS layer states one (observed); no open-data policy, ordinance or executive order was found (observed absence). Two Missouri imagery services carry a reported no-redistribution clause.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Assume public-domain reuse without comment.
decisions.plain: We say plainly that no city dataset states a licence, rather than implying one.

decisions.decision: Use nothing from slmpd.org.
decisions.why: slmpd.org's robots.txt names ClaudeBot, anthropic-ai and Claude-Web with 'Disallow: /' (observed 14 Oct 00:36 UTC), and policing is out of scope in any case (a state-appointed board).
decisions.alternative_rejected: Use police data in the analysis.
decisions.plain: We use nothing from the police department's site, whose robots file bars AI agents; policing is out of scope in any case.

decisions.decision: Respect the city site's robots file: nothing under an address the City's robots.txt disallows, and nothing ending .pdf/.xls/.xlsx/.txt, is fetched by the pipeline; the weekly job uses the bulk files under /data/upload/data-files/, which robots allows.
decisions.why: www.stlouis-mo.gov's robots.txt disallows those paths (observed); research fetched some once, but repeated or scheduled pulls would go against stated policy. A pipeline the city's own robots file forbids could not be the thing the city adopts.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Scrape the catalog's CSV/JSON exports weekly from an address the City's robots.txt disallows.
shows_up_in: README: how the city would run it
decisions.plain: The pipeline fetches only paths the city's robots file allows (the bulk data files), because a job that breaks the city's own crawling policy could not be one the city adopts.

decisions.decision: The pipeline reads the city's weekly bulk files (csb.zip and the forestry ledger under /data/upload/data-files/) rather than the 311 API.
decisions.why: The CSB Open311 API needs a city-issued key and returns HTTP 400 without one (observed); the bulk path is allowed by the city's robots file and the 311 file was refreshed the same day (observed).
evidence: research/data-audit.md 'Read this first' items 2 and 4; section 2 (CSB ds 5)
decisions.alternative_rejected: A live API integration (needs a key the city issues on request; Jack's to request, not ours).
shows_up_in: README: how the city would run it
decisions.plain: The pipeline reads the city's weekly bulk files rather than its 311 API, because the API needs a city-issued key and the bulk path is open and allowed.

decisions.decision: Use the city's board-up layer and demolition permits as independent completion records for 'vacant building unsecured' and land-bank demolition requests.
decisions.why: They are dated, address-level records of the work itself (Boardups 33,141 rows to 8 Oct 2026; Demolitions 3,767 to 9 Oct 2026; observed), the same kind of second record the ledger is for mowing.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Limit the completion layer to mowing and trees.
decisions.plain: We use the city's board-up and demolition records as second records for vacant-building and land-bank requests, the same way the ledger serves mowing.

decisions.decision: Use Cityworks work orders only from the city's public saved-search samples (1,500 rows each, truncated), with staff fields dropped; no wider pull of the city's work-order system.
decisions.why: The city publishes these saved searches as public links; wider work-order data looks internal rather than published (inferred), and the entry should run only on what the city chose to publish. The cost is coverage: the samples hold about a third of the tree work orders, so tree matches are lower bounds.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Pull the full work-order history from the city's wider work-order system.
decisions.plain: We use only the work-order lists the city publishes as public saved searches, with staff fields dropped, because the entry should run only on what the city chose to publish; the cost is that tree matches are lower bounds.

decisions.decision: Use MSDIS aerial imagery only as a visual frame, with no analytic claim attached; check its robots file first; never Google or any keyed service.
decisions.why: Ben's document lists the MSDIS server as a resource (observed). Its robots.txt redirects to a 404, so it publishes no crawl rules, and it needs no key (observed, N5). Its newest St. Louis imagery is 2025, so it cannot show 2026 grass (observed, N5). The 2022 and 2024 orthos carry a reported no-redistribution clause in their bundled metadata, and Google Street View terms bar scraping (observed), so imagery is decoration, not evidence.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Use imagery as evidence of a missed cut, or use Google imagery.
decisions.plain: Aerial images are pictures, not evidence: they frame a block and carry no claim, and we use no Google or keyed imagery. Whether the state imagery's redistribution note allows a public video is still open.

decisions.decision: Use no keys, tokens, sign-ins or POST forms anywhere; the pipeline runs keyless.
decisions.why: Keys and accounts are Jack's to request (AGENTS.md); acceptance test 1 requires a rebuild from public zips with no key. The CSB Open311 API, the address API and CityStat's Tableau export all need credentials (observed).
decisions.alternative_rejected: Request a city API key or sign in to CityStat's Tableau for its underlying data.
decisions.plain: Everything runs without a key, token or sign-in, so anyone at the city can rebuild it from public files.

decisions.decision: 'Missed Cut - V Lot', 'Missed Cut - VBldg', 'Unsatisfy Cut - VLot' and 'Unsatisfy Cut -VBldg' are treated as weed codes and joined to the ledger.
decisions.why: They are residents telling the city a rotation cut was missed or incomplete (city's own descriptions: 'Vacant lot missed on ward cutting rotation'); 12,234 requests since 2009 (observed). They surfaced inside N5's hero cases.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Leaving them out of the weeds family.
decisions.plain: We include the 'missed cut' and 'unsatisfactory cut' request types with weeds, because they are residents telling the city a rotation cut did not happen (12,234 such requests since 2009).

decisions.decision: Convert Cityworks epoch-millisecond dates from UTC to Central before comparing them with 311 times.
decisions.why: 311 times are Central (observed); Cityworks layers return UTC epochs. N5 converted; N1 had not, which moved boundary cases by up to six hours.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Comparing UTC with Central.
decisions.plain: Convert Cityworks epoch-millisecond dates from UTC to Central before comparing them with 311 times. 311 times are Central (observed); Cityworks layers return UTC epochs.

decisions.decision: 'Cut incomplete' and 'missed on rotation' calls stay in the lot timelines as one explicit, neutral line each: who reported what (with the city's own plain-English type name), how 311 closed it, and what the ledger bills before and after. Lot-1's story names the 9 Sep call. A registry figure gives the base rate.
decisions.why: N8 finding 1: a 'Vacant lot cut incomplete' call on lot-1 (9 Sep 2026) would read to a city viewer as 'someone cut it'. Re-derived context (n5_unsat_cut_calls_2026): of 227 parcel-matched such calls in 2026, 63 came within 30 days after a billed cut and 40 were on lots with no cut billed all year (N8, wider join: 229 / 67 / 61), so the call does not show a cut happened, but it must be shown, not scrolled past.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Dropping the call from the receipt, or leaving it as a bare type code.
decisions.plain: 'Cut incomplete' and 'missed on rotation' calls stay in the lot timelines as one explicit, neutral line each: who reported what (with the city's own plain-English type name), how 311 closed it, and what the ledger bills before and after. Lot-1's story names the 9 Sep call. A registry figure gives the base rate. N8 finding 1: a 'Vacant lot cut incomplete' call on lot-1 (9 Sep 2026) would read to a city viewer as 'someone cut it'.

decisions.decision: Ledger history on every lot counts distinct (SERVICEDATE, SERVICETYPE) cut dates, not rows; 2026 cut lists and city-block counts are distinct too.
decisions.why: N8 finding 10: the ledger repeats many legacy rows (2019: 112,734 cut rows, 55,624 distinct). Lot-1 read '2019: 12, 2020: 10' by rows; it is 6 and 5 distinct dates.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Counting ledger rows as cuts.
decisions.plain: Ledger history on every lot counts distinct (SERVICEDATE, SERVICETYPE) cut dates, not rows; 2026 cut lists and city-block counts are distinct too. N8 finding 10: the ledger repeats many legacy rows (2019: 112,734 cut rows, 55,624 distinct).

decisions.decision: Storyboard B speaks 'cuts billed on nearly 12,000 parcels', not '37,543 cuts'; mowing-gap lots are 'more than 90 days without a billed cut (counting to 30 September)'.
decisions.why: N8 finding 10: the ledger repeats rows (2026: about 31,500 distinct parcel-days against 37,543 rows); finding 15d: the gap definition counts the run to 30 September and includes lots cut once.
decisions.alternative_rejected: n1_ledger_2026.rows and 'between billed cuts'.
decisions.plain: Storyboard B speaks 'cuts billed on nearly 12,000 parcels', not '37,543 cuts'; mowing-gap lots are 'more than 90 days without a billed cut (counting to 30 September)'. N8 finding 10: the ledger repeats rows (2026: about 31,500 distinct parcel-days against 37,543 rows); finding 15d: the gap definition counts the run to 30 September and includes lots cut once.

decisions.decision: Say 'for one in five vacant-lot requests closed "on schedule", the ledger bills no cut all year' (revised 1:10 a.m.; first draft said one in four).
decisions.why: N8 finding 2: n1_weeds_lot_onschedule_ledger (0.2475 of 808) mixes in 'added to rotation' closures; for 'on schedule to be cut' alone the share is 21.4% (156 of 729), registered by N1 as n1_weeds_lot_onschedule_only_no_cut_2026. It is a share of requests, not lots.
decisions.alternative_rejected: 'One in four lots closed this way' (the brief's default) and 'one in four requests' (the mixed figure).
decisions.plain: Say 'for one in five vacant-lot requests closed "on schedule", the ledger bills no cut all year' (revised 1:10 a.m.; first draft said one in four). N8 finding 2: n1_weeds_lot_onschedule_ledger (0.2475 of 808) mixes in 'added to rotation' closures; for 'on schedule to be cut' alone the share is 21.4% (156 of 729), registered by N1 as n1_weeds_lot_onschedule_only_no_cut_2026.

decisions.decision: Two research-phase news sources were kept but flagged as droppable: r/StLouis posts from Arctic Shift (a third-party archive with no published terms) and Fox 2 article text read through its public WordPress API after the pages returned 403. Neither feeds the product.
decisions.why: Reddit blocks direct collection; the archive was the only route. Both were surfaced to Jack as his call rather than silently used or silently dropped.
evidence: session transcripts 12bea175 (about 6:35 p.m.) and ea016740 (about 7:40 p.m.)
decisions.alternative_rejected: Use them without flagging, or discard them without telling Jack.
decisions.plain: Two news sources gathered during research (an archive of Reddit posts and article text read after a site blocked direct access) were flagged for Jack to keep or drop; neither feeds the product.

decisions.decision: Use the file's WARD (normalised to '01'..'14'); fill the 3,107 requests with a missing or malformed WARD from the ward polygons (maps8_BOUNDARIES_Wards) by point-in-polygon on SRX/SRY.
decisions.why: WARD is already on the current 14-ward plan in every year, back to 2008 (observed: 1-14 for over 99% of rows each year). On a 20,000-request sample from 2025-26, file ward and polygon ward agree for 99.9% (19,986 of 19,997).
decisions.alternative_rejected: Recomputing ward from coordinates for every row (slower, needs the polygons to be current, and disagrees with the city's own assignment in 0.1% of cases).
decisions.plain: We use the ward printed on each request and fill the 3,107 missing or malformed ones from the ward map, because the printed ward agrees with the map on 99.9% of a 20,000-request sample.

decisions.decision: Cityworks dates (epoch milliseconds) are read as UTC and shown in Central; 311 times are taken as Central.
decisions.why: Under this reading tree-1's 'investigation done' (11:44), work-order start (12:26) and cancellation (12:27) line up; other readings put the work order hours away.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Using the raw UTC dates.
decisions.plain: Work-order times are read as UTC and shown in Central, because under that reading a tree case's three timestamps line up to the minute.

decisions.decision: Retire the raw ward-gap headlines: never use '1.7 vs 27.6 days' (cave-ins) or '98 vs 6.7 days' (tree inspection) anywhere.
decisions.why: Both compared different kinds of closure. Cave-ins, like for like ('work completed'): 9.6 against 25.1 days on rows, 8.3 against 23.1 on distinct requests, but only 35 such closures in wards 1-5, so the repair gap is unproven; share closed 75% against 45%. Tree inspection, 'removal work order created': 125 against 204 days on rows (124 against 190 on requests, only 21 in the north), 1.6x; the headline was fast 'no service necessary' closures in the southwest (observed, 13 Oct about 11:30 p.m.; N1, N3, N5 re-derived). Nuance from N3: the 1.7 vs 27.6 headline compared a desk referral in the southwest with a field process in the north, and the referral itself takes 0.8 against 41.7 days, so 'inflated by mix' understates the north's wait for the first step. The planned replacement lead, single light out, then failed N3's robustness rule; towing holds.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Keep the larger numbers from the synthesis and HANDOFF-2, which the entry had been planned around.
decisions.plain: We retired our own lead numbers ('1.7 vs 27.6 days' for cave-ins, '98 vs 6.7' for tree inspections), because they compared a quick desk referral in the southwest with field work in the north. Like for like, the cave-in referral itself takes 0.8 against 41.7 days, while recorded repairs (8.3 against 23.1 days) are too few in the southwest to prove a gap; of the replacement leads we planned, towing held and single streetlights did not.

decisions.decision: Count requests by distinct REQUESTID, not by CSV rows.
decisions.why: The city's CSV repeats a request once per caller: 349,031 rows in 2024-26 hold 322,104 distinct request ids, about 8% more rows than requests (observed, N2). Medians shift slightly when deduplicated (cave-ins closed 'work completed', wards 10-14: 25.1 days on rows, 23.1 on requests; observed, N5).
decisions.alternative_rejected: Count rows, as the earlier synthesis and COMMON corrections did.
decisions.decided_by: N2 found it (N5 and N3 independently); orchestrator verified; adopted for all as COMMON correction 6
decisions.plain: We count each request once, because the city's CSV repeats a request once per caller and counting rows overstates requests by about 8%.

decisions.decision: 'The closure did not hold' is measured only for durable-fix types (potholes, cave-ins, lights, trees, signs) over 14 days; the broad 30-day figure is called 'came back', not false closure.
decisions.why: Refuse is collected weekly and dumping recurs at chronic sites, so a second report within 30 days often means a new event, not a failed fix.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Present 11,992 re-filed requests (6.3%) as closures that were false.
decisions.plain: We call a second report within 30 days 'came back', not a false closure, because refuse is weekly and dumping recurs; 'the fix did not hold' is measured only for repairs that should last, over 14 days.

decisions.decision: Read the tree address match as a relative rate against a baseline, never as a share converted: say cancelled tree requests appear in Forestry's work orders 'about five times as often as unrelated requests'.
decisions.why: Cancelled addresses match a one-third work-order sample at 10.8% against 1.9% for unrelated requests (observed; N1 on distinct requests: 10.9% against 1.8%), but requests closed 'work order created' match at only 6.8% (N1; COMMON's 2.4% was for all closed tree requests), so the address match misses most true pairs and cannot measure the share converted. N5 then found most matches sit on removal orders already open long before the request (288 of 345), so even 'converted' is the wrong story.
decisions.alternative_rejected: 'Most cancelled tree requests were in fact converted to work orders' (the synthesis wording).
decisions.plain: We say cancelled tree requests appear in Forestry's work orders 'about five times as often as unrelated requests', not that most were converted, because our address match misses most true pairs; and most matches turned out to be trees already on an old removal order, not new conversions.

decisions.decision: Do not lead with single light out.
decisions.why: Its done-class gap (15.6 vs 41.0 days after the tornado) comes from two quarters filed Oct 2025-Mar 2026; before the tornado the gap is 4.8 vs 6.4 and other quarters are level.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Using it as a headline candidate (as COMMON correction 2 suggested).
decisions.plain: We dropped single streetlight outages as a lead comparison, although our own plan proposed it, because the gap (15.6 against 41.0 days) exists only for requests filed October 2025 to March 2026; before the tornado it was 4.8 against 6.4.

decisions.decision: Compare years at the same age when testing CityStat's claim that response times improved sharply in 2026.
decisions.why: CityStat sets 2026 requests, at most six months old, beside a 2024-2026 average that includes closures made years later. Counting only closures by 1 July of each year, the January-June averages are 10.6 days (2024), 10.4 (2025) and 9.2 (2026). Counting every closure to date, 2024 rises to 34.6.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Repeating CityStat's comparison as published.
decisions.plain: We re-tested CityStat's claim that response times improved sharply in 2026 at equal age, because it compared six-month-old 2026 requests with an average that includes closures made years later. At the same age the improvement is modest: 10.6 days (2024), 10.4 (2025), 9.2 (2026).

decisions.decision: Publish no reproduced routing figure.
decisions.why: The file has no routing timestamp, and no subset of it reproduces CityStat's routing request counts convincingly. The best of 260,610 channel-by-category subsets still misses by 4.5% on average and by 15% in 2026 Q2 (12,439 vs 10,853), and many near-ties exist (build/N4/routing_search.json).
decisions.alternative_rejected: Publishing the best-fitting subset (likely a coincidence among thousands of candidates).
shows_up_in: report, the question for CityStat, figure n4_routing_best_subset_mape
decisions.plain: We publish no reproduced routing figure, because the file has no routing time and no subset of it matches CityStat's routing counts convincingly (the best of 260,610 misses by 15% in Q2 2026).

decisions.decision: Two tree cases: tree-1, a request cancelled a minute after a removal work order's projected start (the brief's 'converted' pattern); tree-2, a request filed while a removal work order had already been open 575 days (the median), cancelled two hours later.
decisions.why: Of 345 blank-cancelled inspection requests that match an open removal work order in the public sample, only 9 were cancelled within a day of the work order's start; 288 were filed while a removal order was already open, median 575 days. The common pattern is 'already on the backlog', not 'converted'.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Only the 'converted' case; using the trim sample (no dates; its work orders date from 2019-2020).
decisions.plain: We show two tree cases because the common pattern is not the one we expected: of 345 silently cancelled tree requests matching an open removal order, only 9 were cancelled as the order opened, while 288 were filed when an order had already been open a median 575 days. The usual story is 'already on the backlog, and nobody said so'.

decisions.decision: Claim about residents only what the evidence carries: the wait, the miss, and the city's inability to see what it finished. Do not claim that residents give up, that the status text itself harms them, or anything about votes.
decisions.why: Two tests came back negative: no exit within a year (refuse re-filers filed more later, 63.5% against 46.5%) and re-filing does not depend on whether a cut was recorded (21.2% both ways) (observed). The evidence that seeing completion changes output comes from other cities' audits, not St. Louis.
decisions.alternative_rejected: The strong form: wrong statuses harm residents and drive them away.
decisions.plain: We claim only the wait, the miss and the city's blindness to finished work, not that residents give up or are harmed by status text, because we tested both and neither held.

decisions.decision: Use 3.8% (closed with blank text) and 6.3% (re-filed within 30 days of closure) rather than the research report's 14.6% blank and 23.7% repeat.
decisions.why: Report B's 14.6% is over closed and cancelled requests together, and its 23.7% counts any two requests sharing address and code within 12 months, including duplicates filed while the first was open (observed on re-reading the method).
decisions.alternative_rejected: Quote the report's larger figures.
decisions.plain: We replaced the research report's 14.6% blank and 23.7% repeat with 3.8% and 6.3%, because the larger figures used broader definitions.

decisions.decision: Withdraw the synthesis's own first reading that the harm claim 'fails' because residents re-file at the same rate whether or not a cut was recorded.
decisions.why: Equal re-filing could mean residents ignore the record, that one cut does not settle a chronic lot, or that discouraged residents leave; that test could not tell them apart. Jack challenged it, and a sharper test (exit) was run instead (it found no exit within a year).
decisions.alternative_rejected: Keep 'the strong form fails' as stated in section 8h.
decisions.plain: We withdrew our first reading that the harm claim 'fails', because the test behind it could not tell indifference from giving up; a sharper test then found no sign of residents giving up within a year.

decisions.decision: Stop treating hazard trees as Ben's 'trees' problem.
decisions.why: The written document's tree challenge is canopy and green-space investment; graffiti is absent from it. The spoken 'graffiti and trees' at the kickoff was shorthand (observed in the document).
decisions.alternative_rejected: Keep the earlier reading from the kickoff transcript.
decisions.plain: We stopped treating hazard trees as the city's 'trees' challenge once the written document showed it is about canopy.

decisions.decision: Identify land-bank (city-owned) lots by joining the ledger's PARCEL to the LRA inventory's ParcelId.
decisions.why: The first land-bank join used a column the LRA file does not have and returned '0 in LRA', which was wrong; the corrected join finds 7,425 of 11,972 parcels cut in 2026 are LRA (observed). It also showed city-owned lots are in the ledger, not only billed private lots.
evidence: research/synthesis-notes.md 'Files confirmed on disk' (Correction and addition, about 9:40 p.m.)
decisions.alternative_rejected: The first join's result.
decisions.plain: We found land-bank lots by joining on parcel id after our first attempt used a column the file does not have and wrongly found none; 7,425 of the 11,972 lots cut in 2026 belong to the land bank.

decisions.decision: One normaliser (scripts/night/N1/normalise.py, with tests) for every address join. It follows T-COMMON with two changes: the 'ST LOUIS ... MO 631xx' suffix is stripped only at the end of the string, so St. Louis Avenue survives; and '&' is kept so intersections stay distinct.
decisions.why: T-COMMON's regex turns an MSD address of the form '<house number> ST LOUIS AV ST LOUIS MO <ZIP>' into the bare house number (pattern observed in the MSD file; example number invented). The same function is applied to 311, MSD, LRA, forestry-maintenance and Cityworks addresses. Test cases use invented house numbers on real street names.
decisions.alternative_rejected: The T-COMMON regex as written; a geocoder (needs a key or a network service).
decisions.plain: We fixed a flaw in our own address rule: as first written it turned an address on St. Louis Avenue into a bare house number, so the 'St. Louis, MO' suffix is now stripped only at the end of an address. One tested normaliser is used for every address join.

decisions.decision: Monday brief: the LRA list is resident-filed with N5's headline (94 requests on 75 lots); the tree list matches the removal order at the same address with N5's headline (288, median 575 days); per-ward first-step medians use the published WARD column (cave-in referral 41.7, not 41.1).
decisions.why: N8 conflicts 2, 3 and 4: N5's rule has a registered funnel; within 30 m reaches neighbouring trees; the published column is reproducible from the CSV without GIS.
decisions.alternative_rejected: N1's wider join (103 on 82; 499 within 30 m; filled wards).
decisions.plain: Monday brief: the LRA list is resident-filed with N5's headline (94 requests on 75 lots); the tree list matches the removal order at the same address with N5's headline (288, median 575 days); per-ward first-step medians use the published WARD column (cave-in referral 41.7, not 41.1). N8 conflicts 2, 3 and 4: N5's rule has a registered funnel; within 30 m reaches neighbouring trees; the published column is reproducible from the CSV without GIS.

decisions.decision: The bridge's address scrubber now runs only on address-bearing fields (block, public_address, closing words, receipt story and timeline text, captions), case-sensitively; prose (decisions, negative results, derivations) is passed through as written. Two-number labels (of the form '1234 & 1236 EXAMPLE AV') round to the first number's block.

decisions.alternative_rejected: Scrubbing every string on the page.

Two-number labels (of the form '1234 & 1236 EXAMPLE AV') round to the first number's block.
