decisions.decision: Use Ben's figure for the unhoused population (1,790 in 2026, 323 unsheltered), not Board Bill 91's 'more than 1,700' unsheltered.
decisions.why: The organiser document gives the 2026 count directly and settles the research's open point (observed).
decisions.alternative_rejected: The bill's figure.
decisions.plain: We use the organiser's 2026 count of unhoused residents (1,790, 323 unsheltered) instead of a bill's older figure.

decisions.decision: Read the 311 CSVs with invalid UTF-8 bytes dropped (iconv -c into build/csb-clean/), or with encoding_errors='replace'.
decisions.why: The city's CSVs contain invalid UTF-8 and break strict readers (observed). Dropping the bad bytes loses a few characters in free text and changes no dates, codes or ids (inferred).
decisions.alternative_rejected: Decode as Latin-1 (silently changes characters) or fail on the bad rows.
decisions.plain: We drop the invalid bytes in the city's 311 CSVs before reading them, which loses a few characters of free text and changes no dates, codes or ids.

decisions.decision: Ignore the EXPLANATION field.
decisions.why: It holds only the request type's help text, not anything about the request (observed).
decisions.alternative_rejected: Treat it as a per-request explanation of the outcome.
decisions.plain: We ignore the EXPLANATION field, because it holds only the request type's help text.

decisions.decision: Status groups use upper(STATUS): CLOSED with a DATETIMECLOSED = closed; CANCEL = cancelled; anything else = open.
decisions.why: The file has 'Closed' (4,098 rows) and 'Cancel' (2,381 rows) beside 'CLOSED' and 'CANCEL' (observed). T-COMMON: closed means STATUS CLOSED with DATETIMECLOSED.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Case-sensitive match (would count 6,479 finished rows as open).
decisions.plain: We read the status field without regard to case, because the file mixes 'Closed' and 'CLOSED', 'Cancel' and 'CANCEL' (about 6,500 rows otherwise misread as open).

decisions.decision: One entry with one owner and one ask: answer Ben's written design question 5 ('how can the city better communicate how we're doing on delivering key city services?') with data instead of a mock-up, and make the other findings its pages rather than separate apps.
decisions.why: Ben's written document (received about 9:35 p.m.) put CityStat on his list as written, invites the critique, and dropped hazard trees. Three apps would be three adoption asks and three stories in two minutes. Most entrants were expected to answer question 5 with a design mock-up (inferred).
decisions.alternative_rejected: Several separate tools (mowing, 311, trees, sidewalks), which Jack first proposed given abundant compute.
decisions.decided_by: synthesis session, accepted by Jack ('This sounds good as a first read')
decisions.plain: We built one entry that answers the city's own question 5 (how to communicate service delivery) with data, with the other findings as its pages, because three separate apps would be three adoption asks.

decisions.decision: Satellite verification of mowing is dropped.
decisions.why: A vacant lot is about 300 square metres, which is 3 to 6 Sentinel-2 pixels at 10 m, so a cut is unlikely to be detectable (inferred); GeoSTL reported in August it was already working with the city on satellite mowing priority (reported), so we would be racing them.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Sentinel-2 vegetation-index change on twenty known-cut parcels as a third record (the synthesis's stretch goal).
shows_up_in: write-up: what we did not do
decisions.plain: We dropped satellite checks of mowing, because a vacant lot is only 3 to 6 satellite pixels across and GeoSTL is already working on it with the city.

decisions.decision: Name three end users and give each a door: residents (a public CityStat redesign and the receipt, answering Ben's question 5); city staff (a one-page Monday brief and block-level lists for the weekly data review, as a plain document, not a mock of internal software); the CityStat team (SQL, definitions, and the register as a roadmap).
decisions.why: Jack asked who the end user is. Each audience already has a routine the output can drop into (CityStat's internal operations meetings; the resident-facing CityStat page), and a mock of internal city software would claim knowledge of systems we have not seen. Decision recorded as reversible.
evidence: research/what-gets-adopted.md section 3.2 (CityStat's internal operations meetings, reported)
decisions.alternative_rejected: One audience (the public page only), or a mock-up of the city's internal work-order screens.
decisions.plain: The site has three doors: residents (the receipt and a clearer CityStat), city staff (a one-page Monday brief and block-level lists for the weekly review) and the CityStat team (SQL, definitions and the register as a roadmap), because each already has a routine this can drop into.

decisions.decision: Build the through line (St. Louis records when a job starts and is handed off, not when it is done) as one completion layer, rather than a single-service tool.
decisions.why: Jack asked for the upstream cause behind the separate findings. Two tests on the city's own records supported it: weed requests closed the day they are filed with no cut in the ledger on most lots that month, and tree requests cancelled with no text whose addresses turn up in Forestry's work orders (observed). The same shape appears in towing, water leaks, refuse, sidewalks, the tornado tracker and sirens.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Mowing alone (the synthesis's first pick; it passes every gate and remains the fallback).
decisions.decided_by: synthesis session after Jack's request; Jack 'sounds good as a first read'
decisions.plain: We built one completion layer across services rather than a single mowing tool, because the same gap (closed when handed off, not when done) shows up in weeds, trees, towing, water leaks, refuse and sidewalks.

decisions.decision: Ship one Monday list that is useful this week (requests past the city's own promised date, open, by ward and type, block level, downloadable CSV), not a list per division.
decisions.why: One owner, one ask; the mowing list cannot be live until April because the season is over, so it is shown as a retrospective.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Five Monday lists (mowing, trees, cave-ins, dumping, sidewalks) from the original spec.
decisions.plain: We ship one Monday list (open requests past the city's own promised date, by ward and type) rather than one per division, because one useful list is easier to adopt than five.

decisions.decision: Add view lra_onschedule_no_cut with N5's rule (Weeds-Vacant Lot, 2026, resident-filed, closed within 3 days 'on schedule to be cut' or 'added to rotation', LRA parcel, no cut billed after filing) and register its counts as n1_lra_onschedule_no_cut, noting that public text uses N5's 94 on 75.
decisions.why: N8 conflict 2: the brief's 103 on 82 dropped the resident filter. N1's view gives 96 requests on 76 lots; the remaining gap to N5 is N1's wider parcel join.
decisions.alternative_rejected: A second, all-channel count beside N5's.
shows_up_in: lra_onschedule_no_cut view (N6's bridge.py list a should read it)
decisions.plain: Add view lra_onschedule_no_cut with N5's rule (Weeds-Vacant Lot, 2026, resident-filed, closed within 3 days 'on schedule to be cut' or 'added to rotation', LRA parcel, no cut billed after filing) and register its counts as n1_lra_onschedule_no_cut, noting that public text uses N5's 94 on 75. N8 conflict 2: the brief's 103 on 82 dropped the resident filter.

decisions.decision: Illegal dumping stays as one light page: repeat sites at block level and outcomes by site.
decisions.why: It is Ben's problem set 3 and the 311 file is named as its data, so many entrants will build a hotspot map (inferred); the depth only this entry has is the repeat-address count (959 addresses, 50 with five or more, one with 32) and the enforcement outcomes already coded in the file (observed).
decisions.alternative_rejected: A full dumping chapter with hotspot prediction by time and place.
decisions.plain: Dumping gets one page of repeat sites and outcomes, because many entrants will map hotspots and our depth is what happened after each report.

decisions.decision: Show mowing as a 2026 retrospective, not a live list.
decisions.why: The mowing season is over or ending, so a live next-cut list is not useful until April 2027. The city's own Forestry page says mowing runs 'Between April and October each year' (observed, research G) and the research dates the season's end to 31 October; NIGHT-PLAN's '1 March to 30 September' window has no source in the project files (untraced). The 2026 first rotation started 6 April.
decisions.alternative_rejected: A live mowing Monday list.
decisions.plain: Mowing is shown as a look back at 2026, because the season is over and a live list is not useful until spring.

decisions.decision: Candidates dropped with a stated reason: graffiti (lowest need; not in Ben's written document), heat and planting (tools exist and the field is crowded), potholes (need halved; detection years away), water mains (no mains layer; token-gated), tornado dashboard (duplicates contracted UMSL work), ARPA tracker, ward capital portal, building permits, drones, the crime device and help for elderly neighbours.
decisions.why: Each failed a firm gate or did not beat the baseline on evidence; for example the ARPA exports do not reconcile ($403,080,817 against $101,214,949; observed) and no ward capital spending is published (observed absence).
decisions.alternative_rejected: Keep a long list of candidates open into the build.
decisions.plain: We dropped graffiti, heat maps, potholes, water mains and others with a stated reason each, usually thin need, an existing tool, or no data.

decisions.decision: Sidewalks become one row in the register, not a chapter.
decisions.why: It is a separate data world (inventory, crowd labels, ward funds); the city's sidewalk inventory has DateRepair filled on 0 of 36,822 segments (observed, N2), so there is no completion record to join; and sidewalk money is ward money needing up to fourteen yeses (observed).
decisions.alternative_rejected: The EO 96 sidewalk map and repair queue as a chapter.
decisions.plain: Sidewalks are one row in the register, because the city's sidewalk map has no repair dates at all (0 of 36,822) and sidewalk money needs up to fourteen aldermen's approval.

decisions.decision: Hazard trees become one page (the silent cancellations), not a tool.
decisions.why: Ben's written tree challenge is canopy investment, not hazard removal, so the certificate argument fell away (observed in the document); resident evidence for hazard trees is thin and the constraint looks like crews (tree trimmers 50% vacant, reported).
decisions.alternative_rejected: A removal-backlog ordering tool and 'where is my tree' page.
decisions.plain: Hazard trees are one page, not a tool, because the city's written challenge is about canopy, not removals, and the constraint there is crews.

decisions.decision: Build time is not a selection criterion, and the entry need not be one of Ben's problems.
decisions.why: Jack removed both: people and agents underestimate what can be built with LLMs in a short time, and he did not think it needed to be one of Ben's problems.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Prefer ideas that are quick to build, or only Ben's listed problems.
decisions.plain: Build time and being on Ben's list were not used to rule ideas out, at Jack's direction.

decisions.decision: Stay solo; do not team with another entrant.
decisions.why: Coordination would cost more than it gains with about 40 hours left, and the entry's edge is depth only this pipeline has (inferred).
decisions.alternative_rejected: Join the kickoff team that said it was open to collaborators.
decisions.plain: We stayed solo, because coordinating with another team would cost more than it gained in the time left.

decisions.decision: One figure registry (figures.json), written by the code and read by the site and the script, with a plain-English derivation for every number and a 'How we know' link beside it on the site.
decisions.why: Jack does not want the chain behind any number to stay implicit. A single registry also means a number changes in one place, and the research phase's hand-written facts CSVs had already lost figures (fifteen dropped in the earlier synthesis run).
decisions.alternative_rejected: A hand-written facts CSV per chapter, as in the research phase.
decisions.plain: Every number lives in one registry that the code writes and the site and script read, each with a plain account of how it was derived, so no figure's chain of sources stays implicit.

decisions.decision: Say 'no cut billed in the Forestry ledger', never 'never cut' or 'never mowed'.
decisions.why: The ledger is a billing record, not an operations log; dates are posted in weekly batches; lot-1 drew an 'unsatisfactory cut' complaint on 9 Sep 2026, which could mean someone saw a partial cut the ledger does not show.
decisions.alternative_rejected: 'The city never cut the lot.'
decisions.plain: We say 'no cut billed in the Forestry ledger', never 'never cut' or 'never mowed', because the ledger is a billing record posted in weekly batches.

decisions.decision: Recommend storyboard A (one lot's receipt, then the like-for-like ward finding, then the site's three users, then the ask) and give B (mowing throughout) and C (numbers first) as full alternatives.
decisions.why: A is the only one that meets Mike's personal-story test in the first 30 seconds and Ben's adoption test, and it shows breadth. The ward finding survived N3's attempt to explain it away (research/chapters/N3-fairness.md). Jack approved the lead provisionally (build/INTEGRATION-LOG.md 23:50).
decisions.alternative_rejected: B as the recommendation (clearest story, but one service and out of season); C (most complete argument, but abstract for 50 seconds and can read as an audit).
decisions.plain: We recommend the storyboard that opens on one lot's receipt, then the like-for-like ward finding, then the site's three users and the ask, because it is the only one that gives a personal story in the first 30 seconds (the organisers' test) and a route to adoption (the COO's office's test). Two full alternatives (mowing throughout; numbers first) are written for Jack to choose from.

decisions.decision: Show what we tested that did not hold, on the site and in the write-up.
decisions.why: Two of the project's own tests failed (no exit; status text does not drive re-filing) and three of its claims were cut back (ward gap, tree conversions, re-filing). Showing them is what lets a city analyst trust the rest.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Report only what held.
decisions.plain: We publish what we tested that did not hold, because it is what lets a city analyst trust what did.

decisions.decision: No city look-alike: no seal, no city colours or logo, a footer saying 'Independent prototype built from the City of St. Louis's open data. Not a City website.', hosted under our own name. CityStat's structure appears only in the scoreboard section.
decisions.why: A clone invites the 'derivative of a two-person team's quarterly site' comparison and drifts toward impersonating the city. Jack liked a clone because it shows where each fix would go; the scoreboard keeps that benefit.
evidence: session transcript 93c7fcd6, about 9:44 p.m. ('Do not publish a lookalike of a city site')
decisions.alternative_rejected: A digital clone of the CityStat site with the improvements dropped in (Jack's first idea).
decisions.decided_by: night-v2 orchestrator, from Jack's clone idea
decisions.plain: The site uses no city seal, colours or logo and says it is not a City website, because a look-alike would read as derivative and drift toward impersonating the city; CityStat's structure appears only in the scoreboard.

decisions.decision: Frame the Q3 2026 pothole figure as 'a weekly run would have shown this in July', not 'your potholes collapsed'.
decisions.why: Residential potholes met the 8-day goal 24.3% of the time in Q3 against 84.4% for Q2 in today's file (CityStat published 90.6%), but the four quarters before Q2 ran 42-50%, so Q2 was the outlier and Q3 the low; the cause is unknown. The orchestrator checked it is not a batch-closure artefact (the largest single close day is 12% of Q3 closures). The point the city can use is timeliness, not blame.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Lead with the collapse ('from 90.6% to 24.3%').
decisions.plain: We frame the third-quarter pothole fall as 'a weekly run would have shown this in July', not as a collapse, because the cause is unknown and the spring quarter was the outlier; the useful point is timeliness, not blame.

decisions.decision: The product's face is a per-request receipt: filed, promised, closed with the city's exact words, and what the city's other records show (ledger cut, work order, or nothing).
decisions.why: Mike's test at the kickoff was 'the personal story, why this is important' (observed); the biggest doubt about the through line was abstraction in two minutes. One request on one screen carries the thesis.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Lead with the ward table or a dashboard of rates.
decisions.status: provisional: Jack decides the lead after sleep
decisions.plain: The site opens on one request's receipt (filed, promised, closed with the city's words, what other city records show), because one real request carries the idea faster than any chart.

decisions.decision: Say plainly what the layer does not fix: crews and money, police and 911, shelter beds, permits, identifying dumping perpetrators, and any use of exposed personal data. 'Data does not cut grass.'
decisions.why: The city's own words put its backlogs on crews and money: tree trimmers 50% vacant, Forestry at about 60% of mowing staff, 129 Street Department vacancies, $150M of unfunded water mains (reported). A completion layer makes a shortfall visible and orderable; claiming more would be overclaiming.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Imply that better data will clear the backlogs.
shows_up_in: README: what it does not fix
decisions.plain: We say what this does not fix (crews, money, police, shelter beds, permits), because the city's own words put its backlogs on staffing and funds, and data does not cut grass.

decisions.decision: Pitch the layer as the thing the COO says the city is heading toward, and label every recomputed number 'our definition, from the public file' rather than saying CityStat is wrong.
decisions.why: The COO already says 'right now we don't have a comprehensive asset management program' (30 Sep 2026) and 'That's where we're heading' (reported). CityStat's denominators are unpublished, so differences are definitional until shown otherwise.
evidence: prompts/overnight/T-COMMON.md (CityStat goals: 'our definition, from the public file')
decisions.alternative_rejected: An audit framing ('the city's numbers are wrong'), which invites defensiveness from the office that would adopt it.
decisions.plain: Every recomputed number says 'our definition, from the public file' and the pitch is framed as the asset tracking the COO says the city is heading toward, because CityStat's own definitions are unpublished and an audit tone would put off the office that has to adopt it.

decisions.decision: Every figure is labelled observed (we computed or read it), reported (a source says so) or inferred (our conclusion).
decisions.why: Project rule from the first hour; keeps the city's statements, our counts and our readings apart.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Unlabelled figures.
decisions.plain: Every figure says whether we computed it (observed), a source says it (reported), or we concluded it (inferred).

decisions.decision: Show Q3 2026 values (July-September), which CityStat has not published, under the best-matching definition and marked 'our definition, from the public file'.
decisions.why: CityStat's pages say last updated 30 June (observed); the public file runs to 13 October. Showing the next quarter is the demonstration that the quarterly site could be weekly. Each Q3 value carries a floor because closed-only shares fall as slow requests close (N4). The first Q3 result is striking: residential potholes met the 8-day goal 24.3% of the time, against 90.6% published for Q2, with closing words mostly 'work completed' (observed, N4; cause unknown). If CityStat publishes Q3 before Thursday, the line goes stale (check Thursday morning).
decisions.alternative_rejected: Wait for the city's own Q3 figures, or present ours as the official numbers.
decisions.plain: We show the July-September numbers CityStat has not published, labelled as our definition from the public file and with a floor for requests still open, to show the quarterly page could run weekly. They include a sharp fall: residential potholes met the 8-day goal 24% of the time, against 91% published for Q2.

decisions.decision: Register 'on schedule to be cut' alone as n1_weeds_lot_onschedule_only_no_cut_2026 and n1_weeds_bldg_onschedule_only_no_cut_2026 (share with no cut billed in 2026). Keep the pooled figures and say in their definitions that they pool 'on schedule to be cut' and 'added to rotation'.
decisions.why: N8 finding 2: the narration said 'closed on schedule' while citing the pooled figure (24.8%); 'on schedule' alone is 21.4% for lots (156 of 729) and 32.2% for buildings.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Relabelling the pooled figure only (the narration quotes the 'on schedule' words).
decisions.plain: Register 'on schedule to be cut' alone as n1_weeds_lot_onschedule_only_no_cut_2026 and n1_weeds_bldg_onschedule_only_no_cut_2026 (share with no cut billed in 2026). Keep the pooled figures and say in their definitions that they pool 'on schedule to be cut' and 'added to rotation'. N8 finding 2: the narration said 'closed on schedule' while citing the pooled figure (24.8%); 'on schedule' alone is 21.4% for lots (156 of 729) and 32.2% for buildings.

decisions.decision: Keep 'Public Nuisance Rpt' in the headline denominator but give the headline without it too.
decisions.why: The city's own help text says nuisance complaints are a logging service that closes automatically on submission; 97% of its closures are blank. Removing it moves the hand-off share from 35.2% to 36.1%.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Silent exclusion.
decisions.plain: We give the hand-off headline with and without 'Public Nuisance Rpt', a logging-only type the city closes automatically on submission; it moves 35.2% to 36.1%.

decisions.decision: Counter-example: the land-bank lot on the 4000 block of Ashland Av (Greater Ville): one request on 11 Sep 2026, closed in three minutes, cut billed 15 Sep.
decisions.why: A clean single request with a cut within the week, in the same neighbourhood as lot-1. 38 of 331 comparable requests had a cut billed within 7 days; 106 by the request's own promise date.
decisions.alternative_rejected: The 1500 block of N Taylor lot (cut the day after its 28 Jul request, but only after two earlier requests went 27 days uncut); it appears inside lot-1 instead.
decisions.plain: We show one lot where the system worked (reported, closed in three minutes, cut billed four days later), so the receipt is shown to tell the truth both ways.

decisions.decision: Lead lot: the land-bank lot on the 1700 block of N Taylor Av, Greater Ville, Ward 12.
decisions.why: Two web requests (2 Jul and 28 Jul 2026) closed in 13 and 7 minutes as 'on schedule to be cut'; promise date 30 Sep passed; no cut billed in 2026 while 36 other parcels on the same city block (23 of them land-bank lots) were billed on 15 different days; two neighbouring land-bank lots reported at the same moments were billed (20 Jul and 29 Jul); the lot is on Forestry's maintenance list and was billed every year 2019-2024; no LRA offer or garden permit on it; Greater Ville matches the First Alert 4 account of 24 Jul 2026 (research/synthesis-notes.md R4). Sources: csb.zip 2026, forestry-service-records.csv, LRA_INVENTORY.csv, LRA_OFFERS.csv, LRA_GARDEN_PERMITS.csv, forestry-maintenance-properties.csv.
decisions.alternative_rejected: The 1300 block of Arlington Av lot as lead (more requests, but see n5-lot3-caveat); the 8100 block of Church Rd lot (four requests, but almost no other cutting on its city block, so the 'crews were next door' contrast is missing).
decisions.status: provisional: lead lot for the video, Jack decides the lead
decisions.plain: The lead lot is a land-bank lot on the 1700 block of N Taylor Av in the Greater Ville (Ward 12): two web requests closed within minutes as 'on schedule to be cut', the promised date passed, no cut billed in 2026, while 36 other parcels on its city block were billed.

decisions.decision: Block images are NAIP 2024 (USDA, public domain) by default; MSDIS images appear only if site/config.json sets show_msdis_imagery to true (default false).
decisions.why: Coordinator, 14 Oct: MSDIS terms for public reuse are unsettled; NAIP is a public-domain USDA product.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Showing the 2022–2025 MSDIS imagery by default.
decisions.plain: Block images are NAIP 2024 (USDA, public domain) by default; MSDIS images appear only if site/config.json sets show_msdis_imagery to true (default false). Coordinator, 14 Oct: MSDIS terms for public reuse are unsettled; NAIP is a public-domain USDA product.

decisions.decision: Recommend keeping the name DoneStat; call the resident feature 'the receipt'.
decisions.why: No clash found in eight keyless web searches (deliverable/names.md). The name places it in the Stat family the CityStat team knows. 'Promise Kept' sounds like grading campaign promises.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Promise Kept, Follow-Through, DoneCheck, City Receipt, Was It Done?
decisions.status: recommended; the name is Jack's call

decisions.decision: Name lot-1's 9 September 'cut incomplete' call in the narration ('A September call says the cut was incomplete; closed in a day. … This lot: none. If a crew came, no record shows it.') instead of scrolling past it.

decisions.plain: We say 'no new staff, nothing to buy' rather than 'no new software', because the pipeline is new software and the claim would invite an easy rebuttal; nothing has to be purchased.

decisions.plain: We paraphrase rather than quote the CityStat manager's 'we don't have that tracked in a system', because the CityStat team is the intended operator and quoting its manager against the ledger would pitch against the people who would adopt it.

decisions.decision: Lead the numbers with promise dates and a fairness finding that survives scrutiny: the north waits longer for the city's first step (a tag, a referral, a notice), not for crews. The fairness line planned at 11:37 p.m. (that the city's ward chart mostly reflects closing practice) was withdrawn at 11:57 p.m. after N3 tested it.
decisions.why: The inflated raw gap would not survive a city analyst. The planned twist was then tested: an exact decomposition puts only 12% of CityStat's ward 1 vs ward 10 gap on request mix and closing words (1.9 of 15.7 days), and adjusting for mix does not shrink the gap (N4). What survives like for like is the wait for a first step (towing tagged 12.0 against 36.9 days, promise 5; cave-in referral 0.8 against 41.7; building-code notices 3.3 against 8.4), while, since the May 2025 tornado, most closures that say the work was done show no gap (observed, N3; before the tornado potholes ran 22.3 vs 31.8 days, under the 1.5 rule, N8).
evidence: context/NIGHT-PLAN.md 'What I checked' item 1 and 'What changes' item 1
decisions.alternative_rejected: Lead with the raw ward gap (retired: it compared a referral with a repair); or keep the planned line that the ward chart mostly reflects closing practice, after N3 found mix and closing words explain 12% of the gap.

decisions.plain: We withdrew the fairness line we had planned to lead with, that the city's ward chart mostly reflects how requests are closed, because testing showed type mix and closing words explain only 12% of its gap. The line that holds: since the May 2025 tornado, where the work is recorded as done the north mostly does not wait longer for crews; it waits longer for someone to look (a towed car is tagged in 12 days in the southwest and 37 in the north, against a promise of 5), and what happens after the look is not recorded.

decisions.decision: Say where the AI is, in about ten seconds of narration: AI was the method (one person audited 1.5M requests, 2.2M ledger rows and the work orders in two days, and drafted the closure classes in a form a person can review); the product deliberately runs none.
decisions.why: This is a Civic AI hackathon and the earlier plan never said where the AI was; leaving it out invites the question, and the policy turns a constraint into a design choice.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Say nothing about AI, or pretend the product is AI-driven.
decisions.plain: We say in the video where the AI was (auditing 1.5 million requests and drafting the closure classes) and that the product runs none, because at a Civic AI hackathon leaving it out invites the question.

decisions.decision: Lead the towing comparison with medians (12.0 against 36.9 days), not the share of promises met, until the independent check settles which share is right.
decisions.why: Two derivations of the share closed by the 5-day promise disagree: N3 38% against 11%; the orchestrator's raw recomputation 32% against 4% (different timestamp rule). The medians match exactly in both (orchestrator 12.0 vs 36.9 on 1,299/271 requests).
decisions.alternative_rejected: Quote either share now.
decisions.status: resolved by N8: if a share is used, 32% vs 4% (tagged within the promise, like for like); N3's 38% vs 11% counts any closing words and is retired
decisions.plain: We lead towing with medians (12 against 37 days) because two derivations of the share of promises met disagree; the medians agree exactly.

decisions.decision: The 1300 block of Arlington Av lot is ranked third and its story names the possible explanation.
decisions.why: LRA_OFFERS.csv shows offers on the parcel marked ACCEPTED on 4 Nov 2025 and 29 Jan 2026 while the inventory still lists it 'Available'; a pending sale may have taken it off the mowing rotation. 311 said 'on schedule to be cut' five times regardless.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Ranking it first on request count, or dropping it.
decisions.plain: The third-ranked lot's story names its possible innocent explanation (an accepted land-bank offer) rather than hiding it.

decisions.decision: Pages show the city's own plain-English name for each request type (PLAIN_ENGLISH_NAME_FOR_PROBLEMCODE, most common value per code, from N1's requests.type_name), never the abbreviated PROBLEMCODE; fallback is the code with abbreviations spelled out. Quoted codes inside N5's event text are replaced the same way.
decisions.why: Coordinator, 14 Oct: raw codes such as 'Containr damaged' or 'Illegl Use-Opn Storg' read as internal jargon on a resident page and a staff memo.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Showing PROBLEMCODE, or code plus abbreviated category ('Prpty Insp Exterior').
decisions.plain: Pages use the city's own plain-English name for each request type, never the abbreviated internal code, because codes such as 'Containr damaged' read as jargon to residents and staff alike.

decisions.decision: Charts are hand-built SVG and HTML in site/js/charts.js, with no chart library.
decisions.why: The brief named Vega-Lite, vendored. No copy was on disk, and fetching one would have meant an unattended download. The six charts needed (stacked bar, dumbbell, waterfall bar, line, columns, inline bars) are small, and hand-built marks follow the dataviz method exactly: 4px rounded data ends, 2px surface gaps, hairline solid grid, a tooltip on every mark, direct labels. Works offline.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Downloading vega, vega-lite and vega-embed into site/vendor/.
decisions.plain: Charts are hand-built SVG with no chart library, because none was on disk and fetching one would have meant an unattended download; the site works offline for recording.

decisions.decision: Round large numbers when spoken ('about 176,000', 'over 37,000', 'nearly 4,000'); exact values on screen and in the figure brackets.

decisions.alternative_rejected: Reading exact values aloud.
decisions.plain: Narration rounds large numbers ('about 176,000') while the screen shows exact values, so the script fits two minutes.

decisions.decision: Narration and write-up refer to numbers by figure id ({{fig:id}}) with the current value beside it, so text updates when a figure changes.
decisions.why: Figures are still moving overnight (deduplication shifted several medians); hard-coded numbers in a script go stale silently.
decisions.alternative_rejected: Type the numbers into the script.
decisions.plain: Script and README cite numbers by figure id, so a corrected figure updates everywhere.
